en: *Śata-śāstra*, Fascicle One.
Composed by Bodhisattva Deva; explained by the Bodhisattva Vasu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty.
I prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and beseech the World-Honored One: throughout immeasurable kalpas you have borne manifold sufferings;
your afflictions are exhausted and your habitual tendencies eliminated, such that Brahmā, Śakra, nāgas, and devas all pay you reverence.
I also pay homage to the Unsurpassed One who illuminates the world with the Dharma, who can purify defilements and bring an end to frivolous discourse—
the one spoken of by all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones— as well as the Saṃgha of the Eightfold Noble Assembly of Arhats.
The opponent says:
The verse states "that which was spoken by the World-Honored One. Who is this World-Honored One?
The proponent replies:
"Why do you give rise to such doubt?
The outsider replied:
"I have given rise to doubt because the Blessed One has described his marks in various ways."
Some say: "The Deva of Reed-Knots" (in the language of Qin, "the Deva of Universal Victory") is named Bhagavat. Others say:
Maheśvara (Mahesvara) is translated in the Qin language as Daizai Tian (Mahādeva), and is called Bhagavat.
Furthermore, it is said that the rishis such as Kapila, Ulūka, and Leśapa are all called Bhagavat.
"Why do you alone say that the Buddha is the World-Honored One?
For this reason, doubt arises.
The internal [proponent] says:

The Buddha knows the true nature of all phenomena with clarity and without obstruction, and he is also able to expound the profound and pure Dharma; for these reasons, the Buddha alone is titled the World-Honored One (Bhagavān).
An opponent says:
Other teachers as well can clearly understand the characteristics of all phenomena and can also expound the profound and pure Dharma.

For example, when a disciple of Kapila recites the Sāṃkhya-sūtra, he explains the general and specific characteristics of all wholesome dharmas; among the twenty-five principles (*tattva*), that which is the portion of pure discernment is called a wholesome dharma.

The disciples of Ulūka recite the Vaiśeṣika-sūtra, which speaks of the six categories (*ṣaṭ-padārtha*). Regarding the category of quality (*guṇa*), it states that one should bathe three times daily and perform offerings twice; through the conjunction of fire and other elements, the portion of the self (*ātman*) produces wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*).

The disciples of Īśvara recite the scriptures of the Nirgranthas, asserting that practices such as "scorching the body with five fires" and "plucking out one's hair" which involve the endurance of suffering are called wholesome dharmas.

Furthermore, there are various teachers who practice self-starvation, leaping into abysses or rushing into fire, throwing themselves from high cliffs, remaining in perpetual silence while standing upright, and observing the "cow-vow," all of which they claim are wholesome dharmas.
All such things as these are profound and pure dharmas; why then do you say that only the Buddha can teach them?
The internal [opponent] says:
These are all wrong views, for they obscure right view and thus cannot explain the profound and pure dharmas.
This matter shall be explained in detail later.
The opponent asks:
What characteristics of wholesome dharmas did the Buddha teach?
The internal [text] says:
The *Dharmapada* states that the cessation of evil and the practice of good are the teachings.
The Buddha briefly explained two kinds of wholesome dharmas:
The characteristic of cessation and the characteristic of cultivation.
To still all evils is called the characteristic of cessation;
to cultivate all virtues is called the characteristic of cultivation.
What are the evils?
They are misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind. Regarding the body:
Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
Of speech:
false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech.
The mental [unwholesome states] are greed, hatred, and wrong view.

Furthermore, there are acts such as flogging, binding, and imprisonment that are not subsumed under the ten unwholesome paths of action, as well as the various offenses preceding and following those ten unwholesome paths; these are called evil.
What is cessation? It is the stopping of evil and its non-performance.
Whether it arises in the mind, is uttered by speech, or concerns the undertaking of precepts, to resolve from this day forward never to do it again—this is called cessation.
What constitutes the wholesome?
It consists of right conduct of body, right conduct of speech, and right conduct of mind.
These include bodily acts such as welcoming and seeing off others, joining the palms, and paying respectful homage.
Speech that is truthful, harmonious, gentle, and beneficial; a mind characterized by loving-kindness,
compassion, right view, and so forth—
such various pure dharmas as these are called wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*).
What is practice? In this regard, to have faith in, accept, and cultivate wholesome dharmas is called practice.
The outsider asks:
Your sūtra has a fault because it does not begin auspiciously;
for when masters compose the dharma of the sūtras, they first speak of what is auspicious so that the meaning and flavor are easy to understand and the sound of the Dharma may spread far and wide.
If a wise person reads, recites, contemplates, and understands them, they will immediately gain increased longevity, majestic virtue, and respect.

For instance, there is a sutra named *Brahmaparipṛcchā*—translated into Chinese as *Guǎngzhǔ jīng* (The Sutra of the Universal Lord)—and in such sutras as these, it is said at the beginning that [the teaching] is auspicious.
Because the beginning is auspicious, the middle and the end are also auspicious.
Since your scripture speaks of evil at the outset, it is therefore inauspicious.
For this reason, it is said that your scripture contains errors.
The internal [opponent] says: Not so.
This sūtra is preached for the purpose of severing false views; therefore, it is auspicious.
This is inauspicious; this is the breath of false views, and therefore there is no fault.
Furthermore, because there is no auspiciousness, it is called *sūtra*; if there were even a slight degree of auspiciousness, the beginning of the scripture should have stated that it is auspicious.
In reality, there is no such thing as auspiciousness. Why is this?

Because regarding a single matter, what one person considers auspicious, another may consider inauspicious, or yet another may consider it neither auspicious nor inauspicious; since it is not fixed, there is no such thing as auspiciousness.
"You foolish person, lacking skillful means, you forcibly seek pleasure and give rise to false imaginings, saying that this matter is auspicious and that matter is inauspicious.
Furthermore, because neither self nor other can be found together, it is a sūtra."
These auspicious dharmas do not arise from themselves. Why?
Because there is no dharma whatsoever that arises from itself.
Furthermore, there is the fault of dual characteristics: first, that which is produced;
second, that which produces.
Nor does it arise from another, because its own characteristic is non-existent, and thus the characteristic of another is also non-existent.
Furthermore, because it would lead to an infinite regress, since arising itself would have to arise again.
Nor do they arise together, for both positions entail faults.
Generally, there are three ways in which phenomena arise:
Whether sought within oneself, within another, or within both together—among these three possibilities—it cannot be found. Therefore, there is no such thing as auspiciousness.
The opponent says:
This auspiciousness arises spontaneously, as stated in the *Lavaṇa-sūtra*:
"For example, just as the nature of salt is salty and can cause other things to become salty, so too is this auspiciousness;
its own nature is auspicious and can cause other things to become auspicious."
The internal [opponent] says:
Because it has already been refuted previously, and because the *sūtra* states that the characteristic of salt resides within salt;

furthermore, I have already refuted the notion that there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) arising from dharmas. Moreover, you intend to claim that salt arises from causes and conditions; therefore, salt does not possess the quality of salinity by way of its own intrinsic nature.
I do not accept your words; I shall now refute what you have said by means of your own words.
Although salt is combined with other substances, those substances do not become salt, because the characteristic of salt resides within the salt itself.
For example, the characteristic of a cow does not become the characteristic of a horse.
The opponent says:
It is like the *dīpa-sūtra*.
For example, just as a lamp illuminates itself and can also illuminate others, so too is auspiciousness:
it is itself auspicious and can also cause that which is inauspicious to become auspicious.
The internal [opponent] says:
A lamp is called a *sūtra* because it has no darkness for itself or others.
Why is this? Because the lamp itself has no darkness.
Because light and darkness do not coexist, the lamp likewise lacks the capacity to illuminate.
Since it cannot illuminate, it also possesses the fault of dual characteristics:
first, that which illuminates; second, that which is illuminated. Therefore, the lamp does not illuminate itself.
In the places it illuminates, there is likewise no darkness; therefore, it cannot illuminate others.
It is called "illumination" because it destroys darkness; since there is no darkness to be destroyed, it is not illumination.
The opponent says:
It is called *sūtra* because at the moment of its initial arising, both [the lamp and the object] are illuminated.
I do not say that the lamp arises first and illuminates later; rather, at the very moment of its initial arising, it illuminates itself and is also able to illuminate others.
The internal [opponent] says: It is not so.
For in the Sūtra it is stated that the characteristics of existence and non-existence of a single dharma cannot be apprehended.
At the moment of initial arising, it is called "half-arisen and half-unarisen.
As previously explained, that which has already arisen cannot illuminate; how much less can that which has not yet arisen have anything to illuminate?
Furthermore, how can a single dharma both possess characteristics and lack characteristics?
Furthermore, it is called *sūtra* because light does not reach darkness.
Whether a lamp has already arisen or has not yet arisen, it neither reaches darkness in either case, because their intrinsic natures are mutually exclusive.
If the lamp does not reach darkness, how can it destroy it?
The opponent says:
It is like the *sūtra* on the recitation of mantras for the stars;
if one recites a mantra from afar, it can cause affliction to a person who is distant.
It is also like the shifting of stars in the sky, which brings ill fortune to people.
A lamp is likewise: although it does not reach the darkness, it is able to dispel it.
The internal [opponent] says:
Because it is excessively substantial, it is called *sūtra*.
If a lamp possesses the power to dispel darkness without reaching it, why does lighting a lamp in India not dispel the darkness of China?
Just as the power of a mantra or a star can reach far, the function of a lamp is not so; therefore, your analogy is incorrect.
Furthermore, according to the Sūtra, if the beginning is auspicious but the remainder is inauspicious, [the whole is considered inauspicious].
If the beginning of the scripture is auspicious, the remainder should not be auspicious.
If the remainder is also auspicious, then your claim that "the beginning is auspicious" is a falsehood.
The opponent says:
Because the beginning is auspicious, the rest is also auspicious; because of the power of the auspiciousness of the beginning of the Sūtra, the rest is also auspicious.
The internal [opponent] says:
Because inauspiciousness is predominant, the *sūtra* states that what is auspicious becomes inauspicious.
Since your scripture begins by stating that the auspicious is largely inauspicious, and because inauspiciousness is predominant, that which should be auspicious must be regarded as inauspicious.
The opponent says:
It is as in the Hastipadopama Sūtra.
For example, because an elephant has a trunk, it is called "having a trunk"; it is not because it has eyes, ears, a head, and so forth that it is called "having eyes, ears, a head, and so forth."
Thus, by means of a small amount of auspicious power, one causes much inauspiciousness to become auspicious.
The internal [opponent] says: Not so.
Because it would entail the fallacy of the absence of the elephant, this is a *sūtra*.
If the elephant were distinct from its hands, it would likewise be distinct from its head, feet, and so forth; in that case, there would be no separate elephant at all.
If the parts possessed the whole within them, why would there not be feet within the head?
As stated in the refutation of difference (*bhedakhaṇḍana*):
if the elephant were not different from its trunk, there would be no distinct elephant.

If the whole (*avayavin*) were not different from its parts (*avayava*), then the head would be the foot, because both are non-different from the elephant, as explained in the refutation of oneness (*ekatvakhaṇḍana*).

Since such auspicious matters cannot be found through any kind of causal investigation, how can you say that because it is auspicious at the beginning, it is also auspicious in the middle and at the end?
The opponent says:
If the cessation of evil is itself sublime, why does it not exist at the beginning?
The internal proponent says:
A practitioner must first know evil before being able to cease it; therefore, evil comes first and cessation follows.
The external proponent says:
Wholesome conduct (*kuśala-caryā*) should come first because it possesses sublime fruits;

thus, it is called *sūtra*. Since all wholesome dharmas have sublime fruits, the practitioner who desires to obtain these sublime fruits must cease evil; therefore, wholesome conduct should be explained first, followed by the cessation of evil.
The internal [opponent] says:
Because of the sequential nature of the Dharma, one first removes coarse defilements and subsequently removes subtle defilements.
If a practitioner does not cease evil, they cannot cultivate goodness; therefore, one first removes coarse defilements and afterwards applies oneself to wholesome dharmas.
It is like washing clothes: one must first remove the dirt before they can be dyed.
The opponent says:
"Since you have already spoken of the cessation of evil, you should not further speak of the practice of good."
The internal [proponent] says:
Because it consists of virtuous practices such as giving, it is a sūtra.
Giving is a virtuous practice; it is not the mere cessation of evil.

Furthermore, when a great bodhisattva has already ceased all evil and practices the four immeasurable minds, showing compassion for sentient beings and protecting the lives of others, this constitutes wholesome conduct rather than the mere cessation of evil.
The outsider says:
"Generosity is the method for ceasing stinginess; therefore, generosity should be the cessation of evil.
The insider says:
Not so. If one who does not practice giving were inherently evil, then all those who do not give would necessarily be guilty of sin.
Furthermore, for those whose outflows are exhausted, stinginess and greed have already been eliminated; when they practice giving, what evil could there possibly be?
There may be some who, though they practice giving, do not cease their stingy thoughts;
even if they can cease them, they take virtuous conduct as the foundation. Therefore, giving is a form of virtuous conduct.
The opponent says:
Since you have already explained virtuous conduct, you should not explain the cessation of evil. Why is this?
Because the cessation of evil is itself the practice of goodness.
The internal [opponent] says:
The characteristic of cessation is quiescence, while the characteristic of practice is activity; because their natures are mutually contradictory.
Therefore, it is said that wholesome conduct does not encompass the cessation of evil.
The opponent says: This is indeed so.

I do not say that the cessation of evil and the practice of good are of one and the same characteristic; rather, the cessation of evil itself is the wholesome dharma. Therefore, if one speaks of the practice of good, one should not further speak of the cessation of evil.
The internal [opponent] says:
One should speak of the cessation of evil and the practice of good. Why is this?
"Cessation of evil" refers to the cessation of all evils at the moment of receiving the precepts; "performance of good" refers to the cultivation of wholesome dharmas.

If one were to speak only of the merit of performing good without mentioning the cessation of evil, then there would be no merit when a person who has received the precepts and has ceased evil acts with a mind that is either unwholesome or neutral, because they are not performing good at that time. However, since evil has been ceased at that time, there is likewise merit.
Therefore, one should speak of the cessation of evil and also speak of the practice of good.
Because these dharmas of the cessation of evil and the practice of good accord with the inclinations of sentient beings, the Buddha distinguished them into three types:
the sūtras on giving, precepts, and wisdom for those of inferior, middling, and superior capacities.
There are three types of practitioners:
for those of inferior wisdom, one teaches generosity; for those of middling wisdom, one teaches ethical discipline; for those of superior wisdom, one teaches wisdom.
Generosity is defined as the volition associated with relinquishing wealth for the benefit of others.

Furthermore, regarding the names for upholding the precepts through the actions of body and speech: whether expressed verbally, arising from the mind, or through the formal reception of the precepts, from this day forward one shall no longer commit the three types of misconduct of the body or the four types of misconduct of speech.
Wisdom is defined as the mind being settled and immovable within the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Why, then, are there distinctions of inferior, middling, and superior?
It is because of the differences in the degree of benefit conferred.
One who practices giving provides little benefit; this is called inferior wisdom.
One who maintains ethical discipline provides middling benefit; this is called middling wisdom.
One who possesses wisdom provides superior benefit; this is called superior wisdom.

Furthermore, the retribution of giving is inferior, the retribution of morality is middling, and the retribution of wisdom is superior; therefore, one speaks of inferior, middling, and superior wisdom.
An outsider asks:
"Is it the case that all who practice giving possess only inferior wisdom?"
The internal [opponent] says: Not so. Why is this?
There are two kinds of giving:
first, impure; second, pure practice.
Impure giving is termed the practice of those of inferior wisdom.
The outsider asks:
"What is called impure giving?
The insider replies:
Giving in exchange for a reward is impure because it is like a commercial transaction; thus it is stated in the Sūtra.
There are two kinds of retribution:
present retribution and future retribution.
That which yields retribution in the present life consists of fame, respect, affection, and so forth.
That which yields retribution in future lives consists of wealth, nobility, and so forth in subsequent existences.
This is called impure giving.
Why is this? Because they still desire to obtain [retribution] for themselves.

For example, it is like a merchant who travels far to another land; although he carries various goods that bring great benefit, he does not do so out of compassion for sentient beings, but because he seeks his own profit. Therefore, such karma is impure.
Seeking a reward through giving is likewise so.
The outsider asks:
"What is called pure giving?"
The internal [proponent] says:
If a person, out of love, respect, and the desire to benefit others, does not seek rewards in this life or future lives—
just as the various bodhisattvas and superior practitioners perform pure giving— this is called "pure giving."
The outsider asked:
"Are all those who maintain the precepts people of middling wisdom?
The insider replied:
Not so. Why is this? There are two kinds of upholding the precepts:
The first is impure, and the second is pure.
One who maintains the precepts in an impure manner is called a person of middling wisdom.
The outsider says:
What is impure observance of the precepts?
The internal [text] says:
Observing the precepts while seeking a pleasant reward for the sake of sensual desire, as in the *Chupha-sūtra*.
There are two kinds of pleasant retribution:
first, rebirth in the heavens; second, wealth and nobility among human beings.
If one maintains the precepts while seeking the heavens, one will enjoy the company of celestial maidens; if seeking among humans, one will experience the pleasures of the five desires.
Why is this? It is for the sake of sensual desire.
For example, one who conceals their true nature internally desires the forms of others while externally feigning intimacy and kindness; this is called impure observance of the precepts.
As Ānanda said to Nanda:
"Like two rams butting heads, One steps forward only to retreat again;
Your practice of upholding the precepts Is exactly like that."
"Though the body may observe the precepts, if the mind is led astray by desire, these actions are not pure; what is the use of such precepts?
The outsider replied:
What is called "pure upholding of the precepts"? The practitioner reflects thus:

"All wholesome dharmas have the precepts as their root. One who upholds the precepts has no regret in mind; without regret, there is joy; with joy, the mind is at ease; with a mind at ease, one attains single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*); with single-mindedness, true wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*) arises; when true wisdom arises, one attains disenchantment (*nirveda*); through disenchantment, one becomes free from desire (*vairāgya*); through freedom from desire, one attains liberation (*vimukti*); and through liberation, one attains *nirvāṇa*."
This is called the pure upholding of the precepts.
An opponent says:
If "superior wisdom" is meant, then Udraka Rāmaputra and others constitute the superior sūtras.
If one who practices wisdom is called a person of superior wisdom,
then non-Buddhist teachers such as Udraka Rāmaputra and Ārāḍa Kālāma should be considered persons of superior wisdom. The internal [Buddhist] response is:
Not so. Why is this? Because wisdom also has two kinds:
The first is the impure, and the second is the pure.
The opponent asks:
What is called impure knowledge?
The internal [opponent] says:
It is impure because it is bound by the world, as in the *sūtra* where an enemy comes and acts like a kinsman;
worldly wisdom increases birth and death.
Why is this? Because this wisdom still binds one.
It is like an enemy who first feigns intimacy but eventually inflicts harm after a long time.
The wisdom of the world is also like this.
An opponent asks:
"Is it only this wisdom that increases birth and death?"
Is it the same for generosity and morality?
The internal [teacher] says:
"Taking up merit and abandoning evil" is the *dharmaparyāya* of practicing the Dharma.
"Merit" refers to the retribution of merit.
The outsider asks:
"If 'merit' refers to the retribution of merit, why does the Sūtra speak only of 'merit'?"
The internal [opponent] says:
"Merit" refers to the cause, while "meritorious action" refers to the fruit.
Sometimes the cause is spoken of as the fruit, and sometimes the fruit is spoken of as the cause; here, the cause is being spoken of as the fruit.
For example, it is like saying one "eats a thousand taels of gold. Gold cannot be eaten; rather, because food is obtained by means of gold, one is said to "eat gold.
It is also like seeing a painting and saying, "This is a fine hand. The hand itself does not draw; rather, because the painting is produced by means of the hand, one calls it a "fine hand."
"Attachment" refers to being attached to karmic rewards; the evil [consequences] of this have already been explained.
"Conduct" refers to that which constantly leads people through the cycle of birth and death.
An outsider asks:
What is the dharma of non-practice?
The internal [teacher] says:
Both the *sūtras* on merit and those on demerit are called "abandonment"; "abandonment" means the mind does not cling.
When the mind does not cling to merit and no longer wanders through the five realms of existence, this is called the non-practice of dharmas.
The opponent says:
Merit should not be abandoned because its retribution is sublime; furthermore, it is not for the sake of explaining causes and conditions that the Sūtras were taught.
The fruits of all merits are sublime; since all sentient beings constantly seek such sublime fruits, how could they be abandoned?
Furthermore, as the Buddha said: "O Bhikṣus!..."
"Do not fear merit.
You have not yet stated the reason for this; therefore, one should not abandon merit.
The internal [opponent] says:
The *sūtra* on the suffering at the time of the destruction of merit states:
"Merit" refers to the retribution of merit; "destruction" means loss and ruin.
When the retribution of merit is destroyed, one is separated from beloved things and gives rise to great sorrow and suffering.
As the Buddha said:
"Pleasurable feeling is pleasant when it arises and pleasant while it persists, but it is painful when it ceases.
Therefore, one should abandon merit.
Furthermore, as the Buddha said, "Do not fear merit," because one should practice that which aids the path to enlightenment.
As the Buddha taught:
"One should even relinquish merit, let alone evil."
The opponent says:
Because sin and merit are contradictory,
if you claim that suffering arises when merit ceases, then pleasure ought to arise when sin is produced and persists.
The internal [proponent] says:
The *sūtra* states that suffering exists at the time of the transgression.
"Transgression" refers to the retribution for the transgression; since there is suffering even when the retribution is arising, how much more so when it is abiding?
As the Buddha said:
“Painful sensation is suffering when it arises, suffering while it abides, and bliss when it ceases.

You claim that because sin and merit are opposites, sin should be pleasant when it arises; to this we now reply: why do you not say that because sin and merit are opposites, sin is pleasant when it ceases and painful when it arises or abides?
The opponent says:
Since there is no cause or condition for the relinquishing of constant merit, one should not relinquish the *sūtra*.
You claim that merit is relinquished when the conditions for suffering cease.
Since there is no cessation of suffering within the midst of constant karmic rewards, one should not abandon them.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"One who can perform the horse sacrifice transcends old age, decay, and death; his karmic reward is constant, and his place of birth is constant."
"One should not relinquish this merit.
The internal [opponent] says:
"One should relinquish merit, because it possesses two characteristics; thus it is stated in the Sūtra."
This merit has two characteristics:
it can bestow happiness and it can bestow suffering.
It is like rice mixed with poison; it is delicious when eaten, but bitter when it is being digested.
Merit is also like this.
Furthermore, there is merit whose retribution is a cause of pleasure, yet receiving it in excess becomes a cause of suffering.
It is like being near a fire: staying close to ward off the cold brings pleasure, but drawing closer until it burns the body brings suffering.
Therefore, merit has two characteristics; because it has these two characteristics, it is impermanent, and thus it should be relinquished.
Furthermore, as for your statement that the karmic reward of the horse sacrifice is eternal, this is merely words; it lacks any causal basis and is not found in the Sūtras.
The karmic reward for the horse sacrifice is truly impermanent.
Why is this? Because the causal conditions of the horse sacrifice karma are finite.
If the causes of the world were finite, their effects would also be finite;
just as a small lump of clay produces a small jar, so too,
because the ritual of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) is finite in its karma, it is impermanent.
Furthermore, I have heard that you gods possess anger, engage in mutual strife, and cause one another distress; therefore, you cannot be eternal.
Moreover, your sacrificial acts, such as the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), arise from causes and conditions; therefore, they are all impermanent.
Furthermore, since even impure and pure merit are impermanent, they should be relinquished; how much more so the *sūtras* concerning mixed demerit and merit?
This is because, for example, within the ritual of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), there are sins such as killing.
Furthermore, as stated in the Sāṃkhya-sūtra: "The sacrificial dharma is impure, impermanent, and characterized by the marks of victory and defeat; therefore, it should be abandoned.
The outsider says:
"If one abandons merit, one should not compose sūtras."
If merit must inevitably be relinquished, it should not have been created in the first place; what wise person would pointlessly perform such laborious tasks?
It is like a potter who makes a vessel only to break it again.
The internal [proponent] says:
The Dharma of the Stages of the Path for Generating [the Deity] is like the sūtra on washing and dyeing a soiled garment.
Just as a soiled garment must first be washed and then purified before it can be dyed, the washing and purification are not in vain.
Why is this? Because the sequence of defiled phenomena follows a specific order;
for just as a soiled garment cannot receive dye, one must first remove the stains of transgression, next perfume the mind with merit, and only thereafter receive the dye of the path to nirvāṇa.
The opponent asks:
One abandons merit by relying on which sūtra?
One abandons evil by relying on merit; by relying on what does one abandon merit?
The internal [proponent] says:
The *Nirākāra* (Formless) is the supreme *Sūtra*.
By grasping at merit, one is born among humans and devas; by grasping at transgression, one is born in the three evil realms. Therefore, the wisdom of formlessness is the most preeminent.
The signless (*animitta*) means not recollecting any signs; it is free from all sensations, and the mind has no attachment to phenomena of the past, future, or present.
Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there is nothing upon which to rely; this is called the signless.
By means of this skillful method, one is able to relinquish merit. Why is this?
Because apart from the three gates of liberation, no supreme benefit can be obtained.
As the Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If there is anyone who says, 'I do not rely on emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet I desire to attain knowledge or vision free from overweening pride,' that person's words are empty and lack substance."
Chapter 2: Refuting the Self (Ātman). The opponent says:
One should not say that all phenomena are empty and signless, because according to the Sūtras, the self and other such phenomena exist.
Kāpya, Uruvilvā, and others said:
"The self and all phenomena exist. Kāpya said:

From the primordial darkness arises consciousness; from consciousness arises the mind-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*); from the mind-consciousness arise the five subtle atoms (*tanmātra*); from the five subtle atoms arise the five gross elements (*mahābhūta*); and from the five gross elements arise the eleven faculties.
God is the Lord, characterized by permanence and consciousness; He abides in the center, is eternally present, is indestructible and imperishable, and encompasses all phenomena.
One who can know these twenty-five principles (tattvas) attains liberation;
one who does not know them does not escape the cycle of birth and death.

Ulugā said: "There truly exists an eternal self (ātman). Because of such characteristics as inhalation and exhalation, the opening and closing of the eyes, and the life-span, we know that there is a self.
Furthermore, because it is the locus upon which desire and hatred, suffering and pleasure, wisdom, and so forth depend, we know that there is a self."
Therefore, the self (ātman) is a real existence; how can you say it does not exist?
If one claims it exists yet says it does not, such a person is an evil and heterodox individual; and for an evil and heterodox individual, there is no liberation.
Therefore, one should not say that all phenomena are empty and signless.
The internal [opponent] says:
If there is a self (ātman) and one says it does not exist, this constitutes a false and evil view.
If one says "there is no [self]" when there is none, what fault is there in this?
Examine it carefully: in reality, there is no such thing as a self (*ātman*).
The outsider says:
There truly is a self (*ātman*).
As stated in the Sāṃkhya-sūtra, the characteristic of consciousness (*buddhi*) is the self.
The internal [opponent] says:
Are the divine and awakening one,
or are they different?
The outsider says:
The spirit and awakening are one.
The Inner [Text] says:
"If awakening were a characteristic of the spirit, then the *sūtra* states that the spirit is not permanent."
If consciousness were a characteristic of the self, then because consciousness is impermanent, the self would necessarily be impermanent.
For example, heat is a characteristic of fire; because heat is impermanent, fire is also impermanent.
Now it is realized that [all things] are truly impermanent. Why is this?

Because their characteristics are each distinct; because they depend upon causes and conditions; because they were originally non-existent and now exist; and because having existed, they return to non-existence.
The opponent says:
Because it is unarisen, the *sūtra* states that the permanent is so;
phenomena characterized by arising are impermanent, but the self (*ātman*) is not characterized by arising, and is therefore permanent.
The internal [opponent] says:
If that is so, then according to the Sūtra, cognition (*buddhi*) is not a characteristic of the self (*ātman*).
Cognition is impermanent, whereas you assert that the self is permanent; therefore, the self must be distinct from cognition.
If consciousness and the self were not distinct, then because consciousness is impermanent, the self would also have to be impermanent.
Furthermore, it is impossible for consciousness to be a characteristic of the self.
Why is this? Because the awakening and the practice occupy the same locus, it is called a Sūtra.
If awakening were a characteristic of the self (*ātman*), then according to your doctrine that the self is omnipresent, awakening should likewise simultaneously traverse all five destinies.
Furthermore, since cognition and its activity occupy the same location and cannot be all-pervasive, cognition is not a characteristic of the self (*ātman*).

Moreover, if it were as stated in the *Sūtra* that "the self is equal to cognition," and you take cognition to be a characteristic of the self, then the self would have to be equal to cognition; consequently, the self would not be all-pervasive.
For example, fire has no characteristic of being either hot or not hot; the self (*ātman*) is likewise, and it should not possess the characteristics of being either pervasive or non-pervasive.
Furthermore, if one were to consider it pervasive, there would be the *sūtra* passage concerning the characteristics of sentience and insentience.
If you wish for the spirit to be omnipresent, then the spirit would possess two characteristics:
the characteristic of awareness and the characteristic of non-awareness. Why is this?
Because awareness is not all-pervasive.
If the self (ātman) falls within the locus of awareness, then it is aware; if it falls within the locus of non-awareness, then it is not aware.
The opponent says:
Because the power [of awakening] is all-pervasive, there is no fault regarding the *sūtra*.
Although in some places awakening may be of no practical use, here too there is the power of awakening; therefore, there is no fault of lacking awakening.
The internal [opponent] says: Not so.
Because power and that which possesses power are not different, it is a *sūtra*.
If the power of awareness were present within that which is devoid of awareness, then awareness would both have utility and lack utility; therefore, your statement is incorrect.
If you say that even in a place where awareness has no utility there is still the power of awareness, you are merely engaging in empty words.
The opponent says:
Because of the conjunction of causes and conditions, the power of cognition has utility, as stated in the Sūtra.
Although the self possesses the power of cognition, it must depend upon the conjunction of causes and conditions before it can be functional.
The internal [opponent] says:
It falls into the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) because it is a *sūtra*.
If consciousness (*vijñāna*) has utility when causes and conditions coincide, then because that consciousness belongs to the causes and conditions, it falls into the characteristic of arising.
If consciousness and the self were not distinct, then the self would also possess the characteristic of arising.
The opponent says:
It is like the *dīpa-sūtra*.
For example, a lamp can illuminate objects but cannot create them.
Conditions (pratyaya) are likewise: they can cause cognition to be functional, but they cannot produce cognition.
The internal [proponent] says:
This is not so. Although a lamp does not illuminate objects such as a jar, the jar can still be perceived and may even be handled.
If the causal conditions do not converge, consciousness cannot be obtained, and the spirit likewise cannot perceive pleasure or pain; therefore, your analogy is incorrect.
The opponent says:
It is as stated in the Sūtra on Form (*rūpa-sūtra*).
For example, although a lamp may have existed previously, if it does not illuminate, one cannot perceive [the object].
In this way, although awakening exists prior [to its manifestation], it is not yet realized because the causes and conditions have not converged.
The internal [proponent] says: Not so.
Because its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not cognized, it is called *sūtra*.
If there were no illumination, although a person might not cognize it, the characteristic of form (*rūpalakṣaṇa*) would be cognized by itself.
Since you claim that the characteristic of cognition (*buddhilakṣaṇa*) is not cognized by itself, your analogy is incorrect.

Furthermore, because it is without characteristics (*animitta*), the characteristic of form (*rūpa-nimitta*) does not become the characteristic of form merely because it is not known by a person; therefore, even when it is not being perceived, form always exists.
You claim this is the characteristic of the self (*ātman*); however, one should not consider that which is in a state of non-cognition to be cognition.
To claim that what is ignorant is conscious is incorrect; in your own doctrine, consciousness and the self (ātman) are one and the same.
The opponent says:
The followers of Ulūka recite the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra, stating that consciousness is distinct from the self; therefore, the self does not fall into impermanence, nor is it devoid of consciousness.
Why is this? Because the self and cognition are conjoined.
As it says in the *Gavāṃ-sūtra*: [text follows].
For example, when a person is joined with an ox, the person is said to "possess an ox.
In the same way, because the spirit (*ātman*) is joined with consciousness, intention, and sensory objects, cognition arises within the spirit.
Because the spirit is joined with cognition, the spirit is termed "possessing cognition."
The internal [opponent] says:
The characteristic of a cow resides within the cow; there is no *sūtra* (scriptural authority) stating that it resides within "the possession of a cow.
The characteristic of a cow resides within the cow; it does not reside within "the possession of a cow."
Therefore, although the person and the ox are conjoined, it is not the case that the ox does not act as an ox; rather, the ox simply acts as an ox.
Likewise, although the self and cognition are conjoined, and the cognition resides within the locus of the knower, the self does not act as the cognition.

Your claim that cognition arises because the spirit (*śen*), consciousness (*yi*), and objects (*chen*) combine is incorrect; this cognition cognizes objects such as form (*rūpa-āyatana*). Therefore, it is the faculty of cognition (*jñāna*) alone that is capable of knowing, not the spirit (*ātman*).
This is analogous to fire being able to burn: it is not that there is a person possessing fire who burns.
The opponent says:
It is because of the application of dharmas that there are sūtras.
Although a person possesses the characteristic of seeing, they see by means of a lamp; without the lamp, they do not see.
Although the spirit possesses the capacity for cognition, it knows when employing cognition and does not know when separated from cognition.
The internal [school] says: Not so.
Because cognition itself is that which cognizes, it is called *sūtra*.

Cognition arises through the conjunction of the mind, the sense objects, and the sensory faculties; this cognition is able to cognize various objects such as form (*rūpa*). Therefore, cognition itself is the cognizer, and it is not something merely employed as an instrument.
If cognition itself is capable of knowing, what further use is there for a self?
The analogy of the lamp is incorrect. Why is this so?
A sūtra states that a lamp does not know color and so forth;
although a lamp exists prior [to its illumination], it cannot know color and so forth because it is not of the nature of a cognizer. Therefore, it is only consciousness that can know color.
If one cannot know, it is not called knowing.
Therefore, even if there were the capacity to know, what use would that capacity be?
The opponent says:
Because the spirit is conjoined with the body of a horse, the spirit is called "horse" in the *sūtra*.
For example, because the spirit is conjoined with the body of a horse, the spirit is named "horse.
Although the spirit is distinct from the body, the spirit is nevertheless called "horse."
Thus, because consciousness and the self are conjoined, the self is called "conscious.
The internal [opponent] says: Not so.
The deity within the body is not the horse;
"horse" refers to the body itself.
If you claim that the body and the deity are distinct, then the deity must be distinct from the horse; how, then, can you say that the deity is the horse?
Therefore, this analogy is incorrect;
to use the self as an analogy for the self results in a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
The opponent says:
As in the *Kṛṣṇapaṭa-sūtra*:
for example, just as in the case of "black cloth," although blackness is distinct from the cloth, because the cloth is conjoined with blackness, it is called "black cloth.
In the same way, although cognition is distinct from the self (*ātman*), because the self is conjoined with cognition, the self is termed "cognition."
The internal [opponent] says:
If that were so, there would be no *sūtra* stating that there is no self (*ātman*).
If the self is designated as "knowledge" because it is conjoined with knowledge, then the self should not be the self.
Why is this? I have previously stated that cognition is itself the cognizer. If cognition were not called the self (*ātman*), then the self would likewise not be called the cognizer.
If it is designated by the name of another because of its conjunction with that other, then since cognition is conjoined with the self, why is cognition not called the self?
Furthermore, as for the previously mentioned analogy of black cloth, it contradicts your own sūtra.
In your sūtra, blackness is a quality (*guṇa*) and the cloth is a substance (*dravya*).
A substance does not become a quality, and a quality does not become a substance.
The opponent says:
As in the *Daṇḍī-sūtra*.
For example, because a person is conjoined with a staff, the person is called "one who has a staff" (*daṇḍin*), not merely "a staff."
Although a staff is joined with a person, the staff is not called "possessing a person," nor is it called a "person.

In the same way, because the self (*ātman*) is joined with cognition, the self is called "capable of knowing"; it is not merely called "cognition," nor is it the case that because cognition is joined with the self, cognition is called the self.
The internal [opponent] says: Not so.
There is a *sūtra* stating that there is a staff which is not a staff.
Although the staff and the one who possesses the staff are conjoined, the one who possesses the staff is not the staff itself.
In this way, one knows that within the aggregate of cognition there is no self; therefore, the self is not the cognizer.
The outsider says:
The Sāṃkhya person further states that if knowledge were distinct from the self (puruṣa), there would be the aforementioned fault;
however, in my scripture, such a fault does not exist.
Why is this so? Because awakening is itself the characteristic of the spirit.
I take the characteristic of awakening to be the spirit; therefore, it is always awake and never ceases to be awake.
The internal proponent says:
Although this has already been refuted previously, it shall now be further explained.
According to the *Sūtra*, the conscious self (*ātman*) is not manifold in its characteristics.
There are various perceptions, such as perceptions of pleasure and pain; if perception were a characteristic of the self (*ātman*), then the self should likewise be manifold.
The opponent says: Not so.
The first is that which possesses various characteristics, as described in the *Sphatika-sūtra*.
It is like a single crystal bead that changes according to the color [it reflects], appearing as blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth.
In this way, a single cognition varies according to its objects, such as cognizing suffering or cognizing pleasure.
Although cognition has various aspects, it is in reality a single cognition.
The internal [opponent] says:
If that is so, there is a sūtra stating that demerit and merit have a single characteristic:
"The intention to benefit others is called merit; the intention to harm others is called demerit. All those with wisdom believe this teaching.

If the thought of benefiting others and the thought of harming others were one and the same, then sin and merit would share a single characteristic; likewise, acts such as giving and stealing would also be identical.
Furthermore, it is like a gem that exists beforehand and changes according to the colors [it reflects].
However, since cognition arises in dependence upon common conditions, your analogy is incorrect.
Furthermore, because the pearl undergoes new production and cessation at every moment, its characteristics are not identical.
Thus, your claim that the pearl is a single entity is also incorrect.
The opponent says:
Not so. Although the effects are many, the agent is one, just as in the case of a potter and the sūtras.
Just as a potter produces jars, basins, and the like, it is not because the agent is one that the effects are necessarily one.
In this same way, a single consciousness (ekajñāna) is capable of performing various actions, such as causing harm or benefit.
The internal [opponent] says:
There is no distinct *sūtra* regarding the potter.
For example, although the body of the potter possesses no distinct characteristics, it is nonetheless different from the jars, basins, and other vessels [he produces].
However, there is indeed a distinct characteristic between the cognition that benefits others and the cognition that harms others.
Furthermore, since harming and benefiting are not different from the cognition itself, your analogy is incorrect.
The opponent says:
There truly is a self (*ātman*), because it is known through inference (*anumāna*); this is the meaning of *sūtra*.
Even though some things cannot be known through direct perception, they are known by means of their inferential marks (*liṅga*).

For example, when one sees a person depart first and then arrive at another place, although the movement of the sun and moon as they rise in the east and set in the west is not directly perceived, their movement is known because they have reached those respective places.
In this way, seeing that all qualities (guṇa) depend upon substantial entities (dravya), one knows there is a self (ātman) through the characteristic of inference.
Because the self possesses the capacity for cognition, the self is called "the cognizer."
The internal [opponent] says:
This matter has already been refuted previously; it shall now be explained further.
It is not known that the *Śūnyatā-sūtra* is not the *Ātman*.
According to your doctrine, the self (*ātman*) is omnipresent and vast, yet it perceives only a little.
If the self were truly a knower, there would be places and times when it does not know; in that case, it would not be the self.
"Places" refers to the exterior of the body, and "times" refers to the interior of the body, as well as states such as sleep or fainting, during which it does not know.
If the self (ātman) possesses the characteristic of cognition yet at times or in certain places does not cognize, then it is not the self.
Why? Because it would lack the characteristic of cognition.
If you claim that there is a self (ātman) because of the characteristic of cognition, this is empty and lacks reality.
The opponent says:
Cognition does not exist because its activity does not exist, just as in the *sūtra* regarding smoke.
Just as smoke is a characteristic of fire, though there is no smoke at the time of charcoal, fire nevertheless exists even when there is no smoke;
so too, one should know that although consciousness is a characteristic of the self (ātman), whether there is consciousness or no consciousness, the self should exist eternally.
The internal [opponent] says: Not so.
It is because the spirit (ātman) is capable of cognition that there is sūtra.
If you wish to claim that there is a self (ātman) when it does not know, then the self would be unable to know, nor would it possess the characteristic of knowing.
Why is this? Because, according to you, the self exists even at times when it lacks knowledge.
Furthermore, when there is no smoke, one perceives fire directly and thereby knows that fire exists.
Whether the self possesses cognition or lacks cognition, there is no one capable of perceiving it; therefore, your analogy is incorrect.
Furthermore, as for your claim that there is a self because one perceives it through inference based on common characteristics, this too is incorrect.
Why? Because the Sūtra states:
"One perceives the goer, the act of going, and the reaching of that destination."

If there were no act of going apart from the goer, or if there were no goer apart from the act of going to reach that destination, then seeing a goer said to "reach that destination" would necessarily imply the existence of the act of going.
If it were the case that there is no cognition apart from a self (*ātman*), this would not be so; therefore, one should not infer the existence of a self on account of cognition.
One cannot conceive of hair upon seeing a tortoise, nor can one conceive of a child upon seeing a barren woman; likewise, one should not conceive of a self merely upon seeing cognition.
The opponent says:
It is like a hand grasping a sūtra.
Just as a hand sometimes grasps and sometimes does not grasp, one cannot say that it is no longer called a "hand" when it is not grasping; a hand is always called a "hand."

The deity is also like this: at times it knows, and at times it does not know; one cannot claim that it is not a deity simply because of its moments of ignorance, for a deity is always called a "deity."
The internal [opponent] says:
"Grasping is not the characteristic of the hand; this is from the Sūtra.
Grasping is an action of the hand, not the characteristic of the hand."
Why is this? It is not by means of grasping that one knows it to be a hand.
Your claim that "knowing" itself is a characteristic of the self (*ātman*) is an incorrect analogy.
The opponent says:
There must certainly be a self (*ātman*), because it is the Sūtra that states one experiences pleasure and pain.
If there were no experiencer, there would be no experiencing; the body alone cannot experience pleasure and pain.
Why is this? A dead person possesses a body, yet cannot perceive suffering or pleasure.
Thus, one knows that it is the possessor of a body who can perceive suffering and pleasure; this, then, is the self (*ātman*). Therefore, it is certain that a self exists.
The internal [opponent] says:
If affliction is also abandoned, then the *sūtra* is abandoned as well;
it is like when a knife harms the body, at which time affliction arises.
If the deity who is harmed by the sword also experiences affliction, then that deity too should be annihilated.
The opponent says: Not so.
Because it is without contact, it is like the *sūtra* on emptiness.
Because the spirit (*ātman*) is without contact, it cannot be severed.
Just as when a house is burning, the interior space is without contact and thus cannot be burned, yet it possesses heat.
When the body is thus severed, because the internal deity (adhyātma-devatā) is without contact, it cannot be severed; there is only affliction.
The internal [opponent] says:
If that is so, there is no *sūtra* concerning non-going (*agati*).
If the self (ātman) were devoid of contact, the body would not be able to reach other places. Why is this?
Because the process of going arises from volition and from the movement of the body.
The body is devoid of volition, for it is not a conscious phenomenon;
the spirit is devoid of motive power, for it is not a physical phenomenon.
Thus, the body should not travel to other places.
The opponent says:
It is as in the Sūtra on the Blind and the Lame.
For example, the blind and the lame rely upon one another and are thus able to travel.
Thus, the spirit possesses volition and the body possesses motility; they depart in conjunction.
The internal [objection] says:
Because their characteristics are distinct, this is a *sūtra*.
Just as a blind person and a cripple, by means of two types of contact and two types of mental application, should be able to go according to the nature of things;
yet because the body and the spirit (ātman) do not exist as two separate entities, they cannot go. Therefore, there is no phenomenon of going.
If it were not so, there would be the aforementioned fault of annihilation.
Furthermore, your claim that emptiness is heat is incorrect. Why is this?
Because empty space is devoid of tangibility, subtle heat pervades it.
When the body touches and perceives heat, it is not the heat of space itself; rather, one merely speaks figuratively of "the heat of space.
The opponent says:
It is as in the *Sūtra on the Householder’s Distress*:
when a house is burning, the householder is distressed but not burned;
likewise, when the body is severed, the spirit (ātman) is merely distressed but not severed.
The internal [opponent] says: Not so.
Because it is impermanent, the *sūtra* is burned.
When a house burns, because grass, wood, and so forth are impermanent, they both burn and are heated.
Because space is permanent, it neither burns nor is heated.
Likewise, because the body is impermanent, it is both afflicted and severed.
Because the self (*ātman*) is eternal, it is neither afflicted nor subject to cessation.
Furthermore, since the master of the house is far from the fire, he should not be burned.
According to your scripture, because the self is all-pervasive, it should likewise be subject to destruction and dissolution.
The opponent says:
There must be a self (*ātman*), because the *sūtras* state that it apprehends form and other objects.
Since the five sense faculties cannot cognize the five sensory domains, and these are not themselves the cognizing agent, one knows therefore that the self is capable of cognition.
The deity perceives various objects such as forms with the eye and other faculties, just as a person uses a sickle to reap the five grains.
An internalist asks:
Why does he not use his ears to see the sūtras?
If the self (ātman) possesses the power of vision, why does it not see forms with its ears?
Just as fire can burn and burns everywhere it encounters fuel,
or as a person, even when lacking a sickle, can still cut with their hands.
Furthermore, it is like a house with six openings; a person dwelling within it can see from wherever they are.
The self (*ātman*) is likewise: it should be perceivable everywhere.
The opponent says:
Not so. Because each sense has its own fixed domain, as stated in the *Śruti* (Sūtra) regarding the potter.
Although the mind possesses the power of vision, it cannot see forms with the ear because the respective domains of the eye and other senses are distinct and fixed toward their particular objects.
Just as a potter, though capable of making a jar, cannot do so apart from clay;
so too, although the self possesses the power of seeing, it cannot see without the eye.
The internal [opponent] says:
If that were so, then according to the Sūtras,
if the spirit sees by means of the eye, then the spirit is distinct from the eye.
If the spirit is distinct from the eye, then the spirit would lack the eye.
If the deity has no eyes, how can it see?
Your analogy of the potter is likewise incorrect. Why is this so?
Apart from the clay, there is no jar; the clay itself is the jar.
Yet, the eye and the color are distinct.
The opponent says:
Because there is a spirit and the emotions are stirred, there is the Sūtra.
If there were no spirit, why would saliva be produced in the mouth upon seeing another eating fruit? Thus, the eye should not be able to know taste; yet those who possess eyes can indeed know it.
Furthermore, because a single object is known by both the eye and the body, it is stated in the Sūtra:

"Just as a person first perceives a jar or other objects with the eye, even when the eye is not employed in the dark, they are still known through bodily touch; therefore, one knows that there is a self (ātman)."
The internal [opponent] says:
This is like the case of the blind man, which has already been refuted in the Sūtras.
Furthermore, if the eyes see another eating fruit and saliva is produced in the mouth, why would the other sense-faculties not also be moved?
The body is also like this.
The opponent says:
It is like a person burning a sūtra.
For example, although a person has the capacity to burn, they cannot burn apart from fire.
The soul (*ātman*) is likewise: it can see by means of the eye, but it cannot see apart from the eye.
The internal [opponent] says:
To say that a person burns the *sūtras* when it is actually fire that burns them is false speech. Why is this?
A person does not possess the characteristic of burning; it is fire itself that is able to burn.

Just as wind moves trees so that they rub against one another and produce fire, which then consumes mountains and marshes without there being an agent, so too fire itself is able to burn; it is not the person who burns.
The opponent says:
It is as stated in the *Yathāmanasūtra*.
For example, although a dead person has eyes, because they lack consciousness (*manas*), the deity does not see; if, however, there were consciousness, the deity would see.
Thus, the spirit sees by means of the eye; it does not see apart from the eye.
The internal [opponent] says:

If there is a mind that can know and no mind that cannot know, then knowledge occurs simply when the mental faculty operates through the gates of the eyes and so forth; what further use is there for a spirit?
The opponent says:
The mind does not know itself.
If the mind were to know the mind, this would lead to an infinite regress, because my spirit (ātman) is a single unity.
The spirit knows the mind, yet this is not infinite.
The internal [text] says:
"Spirit" is also the *śruti* (scripture) on the cultivation of the spirit.
If the spirit knows the mind, who then would know the spirit?
If the spirit knows the spirit, that too would be infinite.
In my teaching, one knows past thoughts by means of present thoughts; since the nature of thought is impermanent, there is no fault.
The opponent asks:
What is the *sūtra* that refutes the self?
If the self is refuted, how is it that the mind alone perceives the various sense objects?
The internal [proponent] says:
It is like the *sūtra* on the characteristic of fire’s heat.
For example, just as fire is hot, there is no agent; the nature of fire is inherently hot, and there is no fire that is not hot.
In this way, the mind has the characteristic of cognition; although it is distinct from the self (ātman), it is able to cognize because its nature is cognitive.
Since the self’s cognition is different [from that of the mind], the self should not be the cognizer.
The opponent says:
There must be a persistence of past habituation (*pūrvābhyāsa*), because through the continuity of mental recollection, one produces joy or sorrow at the time of birth and practices the *sūtras*.

Just as a newborn infant immediately knows how to act with joy or sorrow even without an instructor, it is because of the continuity of recollecting past habituation from previous lives that one performs various karmas in this present life.
Therefore, it is known that there is a self (ātman) and that it possesses the characteristic of permanence.
The internal [opponent] asks:
How can you recite the Sūtra [to support this]?
The deity constantly pervades all objects and there is no time when it does not think; from what, then, does this thinking arise?
Furthermore, if thinking were to arise in all places, then thinking itself should also pervade all places; consequently, it would follow that one should be thinking of everything simultaneously.
If consciousness arises in distinct parts, then the self would possess parts; because it possesses parts, it would be impermanent.
Furthermore, the propositions that the self is unconscious, or that consciousness is not the self, have already been refuted previously.
The opponent says:
"Because of conjunction, recollection arises; this is the Sūtra.
If the self and the mind conjoin, recollection arises through the impelling force."
Why is this? Although the spirit and the mind may be conjoined, if their momentum does not arise, then thought will not be produced.
The internal [opponent] says:
Although this has already been refuted previously, it shall now be restated.
If the self possesses the characteristic of cognition, it should not give rise to thoughts.
If it does not possess the characteristic of cognition, it likewise should not give rise to thoughts.

Furthermore, if one knows by means of mindfulness of the sūtras, then one knows when that mindfulness arises and does not know when it does not arise; since knowledge would simply follow from the act of mindful recollection, what further use would there be for a *ātman*?
The opponent says:
There must be a self (ātman), because one perceives with the left eye and cognizes with the right; thus it is stated in the Sūtra.
It is as if a person first sees with the left eye and subsequently cognizes with the right eye; it would be illogical for that [left] seeing to be this [right] cognition.
Because there is a self within, what is seen by the left is cognized by the right.
The internal [opponent] says:
This is answered together by the *Sūtra* on the Two Eyes:
"To know partially is not called knowing."
Furthermore, if that were so, there would be no cognition; furthermore, how could there be universal mindfulness?
Furthermore, if it is through mindfulness that one knows, why then does one not see with the ear?

Furthermore, if that were so, one would be blind; furthermore, just as what is seen by the left eye should not be cognized by the right eye, so too the *ātman* should not see one part and cognize another part. Therefore, because what is seen by the left eye is cognized by the right eye, there can be no such thing as an *ātman*.
The opponent says:
Since mindfulness belongs to the self (*ātman*), the self knows the *sūtras*.
Mindfulness is called a quality of the self; it arises within the self. Therefore, the self employs mindfulness to know.
The internal [opponent] says: Not so.
A partial understanding is not called knowledge of the Sūtras.
If consciousness arises in one part of the self, then the self would have partial cognition.
If the self has partial cognition, it cannot be called "cognition.
The opponent says:
The deity knows through partial knowledge.
Why is this? Although the deity knows partially, it is still called "knowing" because of the deity; it is like the *sūtra* on bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
For example, when a part of the body, such as the hand, performs an action, it is called "bodily action.
In this way, although the self (ātman) knows through its various parts, the self is named after that knowing.
The internal [opponent] says:
If that were so, there would be no ignorance, as stated in the Sūtra:

"In your doctrine, the self (*ātman*) is omnipresent while the mind (*manas*) is limited; because the self and the mind conjoin, cognition arises in the self, and this cognition is equal in extent to the mind."
If you claim that the spirit is known because it possesses a small measure of knowledge, why do you not say that the spirit is unknown because it lacks a great deal of knowledge?
Furthermore, as for your analogy regarding bodily action, that is not the case.
Why is this? Because the identity or difference between the part and the whole cannot be established.
The opponent says:
It is as with the *sūtra* on the burning of a portion of a garment:
for example, if one part of a garment is burned, it is called a "burned garment.
In the same way, although the self (*ātman*) knows only a single part, it is called the "knowing self."
The internal [opponent] says:
Burning is likewise explained in the Sūtra.
If one part of a garment is burned, it is not called "burned," but should rather be called "partially burned."
If you claim that a garment is called "burnt" because one part of it has been burnt, then since most of it is not burnt, it should be called "unburnt. Why?
Because this garment is mostly unburnt and remains functionally useful.
Therefore, do not become attached to words.
Chapter Three: Refuting the One Nature. The opponent says:
There must be a self (ātman).
There is a jar and so forth; because it belongs to a deity, it is called a *sūtra*.
If there is a deity, then there is that which belongs to the deity; if there is no deity, then there is nothing that belongs to the deity.
[The opponent says: "There is a jar and so forth that belong to a deity; therefore, a deity exists.
[The internal proponent] says: Not so.
Why is this? Because the self (ātman) cannot be apprehended.
Now, when one contemplates that there exists a jar or the like, does it exist as a unity?
If it exists as something distinct,
both positions entail faults.
The opponent says:
There is the case of a single jar and so forth; if there were a single existence, what fault would there be?
The internal [opponent] says:
If there were one jar as one, then either everything would be established or nothing would be established, or else it would result in the inversion of the sūtras.
If there were only one "Bhagavān," then just as with Indra, Śakra, and Kauśika—wherever there is Indra, there is also Śakra and Kauśika.
In this way, wherever there is existence (*sat*), there is one jar; wherever there is one place, there is the existence of a jar; and wherever there is a jar, there is oneness.

If that were so, then cloth and other such things would also be jars, because they possess the oneness of a jar. Thus, all things that possess oneness would have to be jars; consequently, jars, cloth, and all other objects would now all be one and the same.
Furthermore, because existence is permanent, a single jar should also be permanent.
Furthermore, if one says "existence," one is saying "a single jar.
Furthermore, "one" is a number; therefore, the existence of a jar should also be a number.
Furthermore, if the pot consists of five parts, then "oneness" (ekatva) should also consist of five parts.
If the pot possesses form and resistance, then "oneness" should likewise possess form and resistance.
If the jar is impermanent, then existence (*sattā*) must also be impermanent.
This is called "the proof of everything by means of a single instance" (*ekasmin sarvasiddhi*).
If in every place where [existence] is present there is no jar, then the jars in all those places are likewise non-existent, because existence is not different [from them].
Furthermore, in each instance there is that which is not the jar; thus, the present jar is not the jar, because it is not different from "existence.
Furthermore, if one says that "existence" does not encompass a single jar, then even the statement of a single jar should not encompass that single jar, because it is not different from "existence."
Furthermore, if there were that which is not a jar,
then the jar would also not be a jar,
because they would not be different.
This is called the failure of everything to be established as being "one.
If you wish to speak of a jar, you should speak of existence; if you wish to speak of existence, you should speak of a jar.
Furthermore, because your jar is established, existence is also established.
If one thing is established, then the jar should also be established, because they are one and the same.
This is called "being like one. Regarding all such inversions, the four pages of this section explaining names contain nothing that can be translated.
The opponent says:
Because things possess "oneness," there is no fault in the *sūtra*.
A thing exists and it is also one; therefore, wherever a jar is present, "oneness" must necessarily be present, though not every place where "oneness" is present is a jar.
Furthermore, if one speaks of a "jar," it should be understood that this already includes "existence"; however, speaking of "existence" does not necessarily include the jar.
The internal [opponent] says:
The jar has two [aspects].
Why are there two? Because of the *sūtra* on the non-existence of a jar.
If there were one jar, why would there be a place where a jar does not exist?
Furthermore, how can it be said that there is a jar not subsumed [by its parts]?
The opponent says:
Because the jar exists determinately within the jar, this is stated in the Sūtra.

The pot within the [outer] pot is not different from the pot itself, yet it is distinct from clothing and other such objects; therefore, wherever there is a pot, there is the existence of a pot within it, and wherever there is the existence of a pot, there is a pot therein—not that a pot exists in every single location.
The internal [opponent] says: Not so;
because the jar is not different [from its parts], there is a sūtra.
There is this universal characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa). Why is this?
Because if one says "it exists," then one believes in various things such as jars and the like.
If one speaks of a "jar," one does not believe that it is the same as other objects such as a "cloth.
Therefore, the jar is a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), whereas "existence" is a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); how could they be one?
The opponent says:
As in the *Sūtra* on Father and Son:

for example, just as one person is both son and father, so too is the general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), and the particular characteristic is also the general characteristic.
The internal [proponent] says: Not so.
You are the son; your father is the Sūtra.
If one has not yet fathered a son, one is not called a father; only after the son is born does one become a father.
Furthermore, this analogy applies to me, but it does not apply to you.
The opponent says:
The pot must exist, because everyone has faith [in its existence]; this is a *sūtra*.
People of the world see with their own eyes and believe in the utility of the pot; therefore, the pot must exist.
The internal [opponent] says:
Because there is no difference [between the particular and existence], all *sūtras* would be non-existent.
If the jar were not different from existence, the jar would have to be a universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) rather than a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Since particular characteristics do not exist, universal characteristics also do not exist; it is because particular characteristics exist that universal characteristics exist. If there were no particular characteristics, there would be no universal characteristics.
Because these two do not exist, everything is non-existent.
The opponent says:
For example, the *sūtra* titled "The Body" [refers to] parts such as the feet.
Just as the parts such as the head and feet, though not different from the body, do not mean that the feet alone constitute the body;
so too, although the jar and its existence are not different, the jar is not the universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).
The internal [opponent] says:
If the foot were not different from the body, why would the foot not perform the functions of the head?
Sūtra. If the head, the feet, and so forth were not different from the body, then the foot ought to be the head, because both are non-different from the body.
Because Indra and Śakra are not different, Indra is Śakra.
The opponent says:
There is no fault in the Sūtra because the various parts are distinct.
The parts and the possessor of parts are not different, yet the parts are not non-different from one another; therefore, the head and the feet are not a single entity.
The internal [opponent] says:
If that were so, there would be no *sūtra* on the non-existence of the body.

If the feet were different from the head, and the head were different from the parts such as the feet, then there would merely be these various parts, and nothing further existing that could be designated by the name "body.
The opponent says: Not so.
Because many causes manifest as a single effect, it is like the *sūtra* on the pot and its color and so forth.

Just as the various parts such as color and the rest manifest as the single effect of one pot, herein it is not that color alone constitutes the pot, nor is it that the pot exists apart from color; therefore, the parts such as color do not constitute a single [entity].
The same applies to the feet and so forth in relation to the body.
The internal [opponent] says:
Just as with form and so forth, a jar is not a single *sūtra*.
If the jar were not different from its five constituents—form, sound, smell, taste, and touch—one could not speak of "a single jar.
If one speaks of "a single jar," then the constituent of form and the others would also have to be one, because form and the other constituents are not different from the jar.
The opponent says:
It is like the *sūtra* on the army and the forest.

When many elements—elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—are combined, they are called an "army"; likewise, when many trees such as pines and cypresses are combined, they are called a "forest. It is not that a single pine constitutes a forest, yet the forest does not exist apart from the pines.
The army is also like this.
In this way, a single color is not called a "pot," nor is it the case that the pot exists apart from its colors.
The opponent says:
The *saṃgha* is also like the *sūtra* regarding the jar.
If pines, cedars, and so forth were not distinct from the forest, one should not speak of "one forest.
If one speaks of "one forest," then the pines, cedars, and so forth should also be one, because they are not distinct from the forest.
Just as the roots, trunk, branches, nodes, flowers, and leaves of a pine tree should be analyzed in this way,
so too should all things, such as armies and the like, be analyzed until they are completely deconstructed.
The opponent says:
Because one perceives many jars, it is a *sūtra*.
You claim that since the *sūtras* such as the "Analysis of Matter" (*Rūpavibhaṅga*) are many, the jar must also be many; therefore, you wish to refute a single jar while accepting many jars.
The internal [opponent] says:
It is not because there are many forms (*rūpa*) and so forth that there are many jars (*ghaṭa*);
rather, I am pointing out your error, not asserting that there are many jars.
You yourself have stated that the parts of form and so forth are many, and that there is no separate entity called a "jar" that serves as the effect of those forms and so forth.
The opponent says:
There is indeed an effect, because the cause is not destroyed.
Because there is a cause, the effect is established; this is the *sūtra*.
You destroy the effect, which is the jar, but you do not destroy the causes of the jar, such as its form (*rūpa*) and other qualities.
Wherever there is a cause, there must be an effect; there is no cause that is without an effect.
Furthermore, the atoms that are the causes of a jar such as color and so forth are the effects [of those causes]; since you accept color and so forth, both cause and effect are established.
The internal [opponent] says:
If the effect does not exist, the cause also does not exist; this is according to the Sūtra.
Just as a jar is not different from its many parts such as color and so forth, the jar should not be one.
Now, since the many parts such as color and so forth are not different from the jar, color and so forth should not be many.

Furthermore, as you have stated that there is no cause without an effect, now that the effect is refuted, the cause is also refuted of its own accord, because in your doctrine, cause and effect are one.
Moreover, the three times constitute a single *sūtra*.
When it is a lump of clay, that is the present; when it is a jar, that is the future; when it is earth, that is the past.
If cause and effect were one, then the jar and the earth would have to exist within the lump of clay; therefore, the three periods of time would be one.
That which has been done, is being done, and will be done—such a statement is refuted.
The opponent says: Not so.
Because cause and effect are established through mutual dependence, it is like the *sūtra* on long and short.

Just as one perceives "short" in dependence upon "long," and perceives "long" in dependence upon "short," so too is a lump of clay a cause when viewed in relation to a jar, yet it is an effect when viewed in relation to the earth.
The internal [opponent] says:
Because it would entail the common fault of contradicting others, there is no characteristic of length within length, nor is there a sūtra concerning shortness or that which is common to both.
If a characteristic of length truly exists, does it exist within length?
Whether it exists within the intermediate state,
