or whether it coexists with the intermediate state— neither is possible.
Why is this? Within length there is no characteristic of length, because it depends on something else; it is designated as "long" only by reason of the short.
Within the short, too, there is no length, because their essential natures are mutually contradictory.
If there were length within shortness, it would not be called "short.
If both length and shortness were present within the "middle," there would likewise be no length, as both positions entail the aforementioned faults.
Whether length exists within [the middle] or shortness exists within [the middle], the faults have already been explained.
The characteristic of shortness is likewise so.
If there were neither long nor short, how could they exist in mutual dependence?

Chapter Four: Refuting the Distinct. The opponent says:
You previously stated that there is a distinct pot; this too is erroneous. What is the error?
The internal [opponent] says:
If there were identity or difference, there would be no *sūtra* for each individual case.
If there were one jar, it would not exist as distinct from each [other jar].
If the jar were different from existence, this jar would neither exist nor be one.
If existence were different from the single jar, it would neither be the jar nor be one.
If oneness were different from the existent jar, it would neither be the jar nor exist.
Thus, each [entity] would be lost.
Furthermore, if a jar were lost, that which exists [within it] should not be lost;
yet since that which exists is lost, the single jar should not be lost.
If there were a single [substance], then when the pot perishes,
it should not perish,
because they are distinct— just as when this person dies, that person should not die.
The opponent says:
Not so. Because there is a "one-ness" (ekatva), there is the formation of a single jar; this is stated in the Sūtra.

Although "oneness" and "existence" differ within a single jar, because the jar is conjoined with existence, the jar is called "existent," and because the jar is conjoined with oneness, the jar is called "one.
Your claim that while the jar is lost, "oneness" and "existence" should not be lost is an incorrect statement.
Why is this? Because they are distinct and yet conjoined.
There are three kinds of distinction:
First, the alteration of combination;
second, the alteration of distinction;
third, the alteration of transformation.
Conjunction refers to things such as substances (*dravya*) and qualities (*guṇa*).
Distinction refers to things such as this person and that person.
Transformation refers to things such as a lump of cow dung changing into a lump of ash.
Because they are combined with distinct [attributes], if the jar loses its unity, it is also lost; if unity is lost, the jar is also lost. Since it possesses permanence, it is not lost.
The internal [opponent] says:
If that were so, there would be many jars in the Sūtra.
Because the jar is conjoined with existence, there is a jar; because the jar is conjoined with oneness, it is one jar; furthermore, the jar is also a jar, and thus there are many jars.

As for your claim that because substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*) are distinct through conjunction, the loss of oneness entails the loss of the jar, and the loss of the jar entails the loss of oneness—I wish to refute your notion of distinction; how can you use distinction as proof for distinction?
One should further state the reason.
The opponent says:
Because it is a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and because it is a quality (*guṇa*), there exists a "being" (*sat*) that is not a jar; this is the *sūtra*.
Because it possesses this universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), it is not a jar; because "oneness" (*ekatva*) is a quality (*guṇa*), it is not a jar; a jar is a substance (*dravya*).
The internal [opponent] says:
If that were so, there would be no sūtra on the non-existence of the jar.

If it is not a jar because it possesses this universal characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa), and if it is not a jar because oneness is a quality (guṇa), and if the jar is a substance (dravya) and thus neither existent nor one—then there is no jar at all.
The opponent says:
You accept the *sūtra* on "many jars.
Previously you spoke of "many jars" with the intent to refute "one jar," yet now you again accept "many jars."
The internal [opponent] says:
Since "one" does not exist, "many" also does not exist; this is according to the Sūtra.
You say that because the jar is conjoined with existence, the jar exists; because the jar is conjoined with oneness, it is one jar; and furthermore, the jar is also a jar.
If that were so, when one speaks of "one jar" in the world, you would consider it to be many jars; thus, one jar becomes many jars.
Since one becomes many, there is no such thing as a single jar. Because the single jar does not exist, the many also do not exist, for the many presuppose the prior existence of the one.
Furthermore, because the initial number does not exist, there is no *sūtra*.
Regarding the dharma of numbering, the first is "one. If "one" were different from the jar, then the jar would not be one; and since "one" does not exist, "many" likewise does not exist.
The opponent says:
Because the jar is conjoined with existence (*sat*), it is a *sūtra*.
Because the jar is conjoined with existence, the jar is called "existent," but this does not mean that all things are existent.
In this way, because the jar is conjoined with "one," the jar is called "one," yet it is not entirely one.
The internal [opponent] says:
There is merely this statement; this matter has already been refuted previously. If there were that which is not a jar, then there would be no jar.
Now I shall further explain the *sūtra* on how a jar should not be a jar:
If a jar exists because it is conjoined with existence, then that existence is not the jar.
If the jar were conjoined with non-jar-ness, why would the jar not become a non-jar?
The opponent says:
Because there is no conjunction with non-existence, it is not the case that the *sūtra* [states] "it is not a jar.
The term "not a jar" means the absence of a jar; since there is no existence, there is no conjunction. Therefore, a jar does not become a non-jar.
Now, because existence exists, there must be conjunction; because there is conjunction, the jar exists.
The internal [opponent] says:
Now, because there is the conjunction with the jar, there is the Sūtra.
If it were not the pot, it would not exist; if it did not exist, there would be no conjunction. Now, because there is the conjunction with the pot, existence must belong to the pot.

If you claim that the pot does not exist because it has not yet conjoined with existence, and that because it does not exist there is no conjunction—then, as previously stated, since the entity does not exist, there is no conjunction.
In this way, when the jar has not yet conjoined with existence (*bhāva*), it does not exist; and because it does not exist, it should not conjoin with existence.
The opponent says: Not so.
Because of the existence of jars and other such things, it is like the *sūtra* on the lamp:
their existence is not merely the cause of jars and other objects, but they can also make jars and other objects known, just as a lamp can illuminate various objects.
In this way, because there is that which can cognize the jar, one knows that the jar exists.
The internal [opponent] says:
If there is a dharma capable of cognizing like a lamp, then the *sūtra* concerning the jar must have existed previously.
If it were the case that objects already exist first and are subsequently illuminated by a lamp,
then objects such as jars should already exist prior to their being joined together.
If it already existed beforehand, what would be the use of its subsequent arising?

If things such as jars do not exist prior to their conjunction, yet come to exist because of conjunction, then this existence is a productive cause (*kāraka-hetu*), not a revealing cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*).
Furthermore, if existence is established by means of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*), why does one [characteristic] not become two *sūtras*?

If you claim that a jar exists because it possesses the characteristic of being a jar, then if the object consisting of the characteristic and the characterized is separated, it cannot be established; therefore, existence itself undergoes transformation and possesses characteristics.
If there were no further cognition to cognize a phenomenon as existing, then jars and other such things would also have to be so.
The analogy of the lamp has already been refuted.
Furthermore, just as a lamp illuminates itself without depending on external illumination;
The jar also exists inherently, without depending on external existence.
The opponent says:
It is like the *sūtra* on the characteristics of the body.
Just as one knows there is a body by means of its constituent parts such as the feet, yet the feet do not further seek out their own characteristics;
so too, because existence is characterized as a jar, one knows there is a jar, yet existence does not further seek out its own characteristics.
The internal [opponent] says:
If the parts possess the whole within themselves, why is it that there is no foot within the head, as stated in the Sūtra?
Furthermore, if there is a bodily phenomenon within the parts such as the feet, does it exist there in its entirety?
Is it present in parts?
If it were present in its entirety, there would have to be feet within the head, because the nature of the body is one.
Nor is it the case that it is present in parts.
Why is this so? Because there is the *avayavin* (the whole) and the *avayava* (the parts), as explained in the Sūtra.

If the *avayavin* within the foot were identical to the foot-parts, and the same were true for the other parts, then the *avayavin* and the parts would be one and the same; therefore, there would be no such thing as a *avayavin* called "body."
In this way, since the parts such as the feet exist inherently, the whole (*avayavin*) is likewise refuted.
Because the whole does not exist, the parts also do not exist.
The opponent says:
Not so; because atoms exist, the sūtras are not without their constituent parts.
Why is this? Because atoms have no parts and do not exist within parts.
Since it is through the aggregation of atoms that effects such as jars can be produced, there must therefore be "possessors of parts" (avayavin).
The internal [opponent] says:
If the collection constitutes a jar, then all jars are *sūtras*.
Your statement that atoms have no parts is merely words; it shall be refuted later. For now, I shall briefly explain.
When atoms aggregate to form a jar, if they all aggregate to form the jar, then all atoms should be the jar.
If they do not all aggregate to form the jar, then none of them are the jar.
The outsider says:
"Just as the power of a collection of threads [produces cloth], so too is it with atoms; this is the Sūtra."
Just as a single thread cannot restrain an elephant and a single drop of water cannot fill a jar, yet when many are gathered together they can, so too,
through the accumulation of atoms, their combined power is able to form a jar.
The internal [opponent] says: Not so;
for the sūtra is indeterminate.

For example, just as each individual barren woman cannot bear a child, each individual blind person cannot see forms, and a single grain of sand cannot yield oil, even when gathered in great quantities, they likewise cannot do so.
In this way, neither a single atom can [accomplish the task], nor can many together.
The opponent says:
Since each part possesses power, it is not the case that the *sūtra* is indeterminate.
Individual strands and drops possess power that can restrain an elephant or fill a jar.

However, because individual parts of a barren woman, a blind person, or sand lack power, even when combined in great numbers they remain powerless. Therefore, [the argument] is not inconclusive; one should not use the barren woman, the blind person, or the sand as analogies.
The internal [opponent] says:
Because of the fault of identity or difference between the part and the whole, [this is not a] sūtra.
Whether the part and the whole are identical or different, this fault has already been refuted previously.
Furthermore, because the possessor of parts (*sāvayava*) does not exist, the parts (*avayava*) themselves do not exist either.
If the possessor of parts does not yet exist, the parts cannot be apprehended; how then could they possess the power of action?
If the possessor of parts already exists, what use would there be for the power of the parts?
The opponent says:
You are a person who destroys the Dharma, a destroyer of the sūtras.
All people of the world perceive various objects such as jars; yet you refute them through various causes and conditions. Therefore, you are a person who destroys the Dharma.
The internal [opponent] says: Not so.
You say that existence is different from the jar; I say that if existence were different from the jar, then there would be no jar.
Furthermore, regarding the *sūtra* that states, "To see existence as non-existence,
and to see non-existence as existence [is wrong view]," you are identical to those who destroy the Dharma, and indeed even more so. Why is this?

The head, feet, and other parts combine to manifest as this body; yet you claim it is not the body, asserting that apart from these, there exists a separate "entity" (bhāva) which constitutes the body.
Furthermore, the wheels, axle, and so forth combine to manifest as a chariot; yet you claim that apart from these, there exists a separate chariot.
Therefore, you are a speaker of falsehood.
5. Chapter Five: Refuting Sentient Beings. An opponent says:
There must certainly exist a self and its attributes, because they are presently perceived; this is stated in the Sūtras.

Cognition arises from the conjunction of the sense faculty, the object, and the mind; this cognition is a present cognition. Because this cognition truly exists, the sense faculty, the object, and the mind must exist.
The internal [opponent] says:
Once color has been seen, what is the use of producing cognition through the study of the Sūtras?
If the eye first sees a form and only afterwards does cognition arise, then what further use would cognition have?
If cognition were to arise first and only afterwards the eye see the form, that too is not the case.
Why is this? If one does not see form, because the causes and conditions do not exist, there is also no arising; thus it is said in the Sūtra:
"If the eye does not first see form, then the causes and conditions do not conjoin. Because they do not conjoin, one knows that arising should not occur."
You state that cognition arises because the object, the sense faculty, and the mind come together; however, if cognition were to arise when they are not in conjunction, that would be incorrect.
The opponent asks:
"If they were to arise simultaneously, what fault would there be?"
The internal [opponent] says:
If they were to arise simultaneously, this would not be the case.
Arising and non-arising do not coexist at one time, because of the existence [of the former] and the non-existence [of the latter], as has already been refuted previously in the Sūtra.

If it is seen that [the cause] exists prior [to the effect], they would arise simultaneously in mutual dependence; yet if it were non-existent prior, or if it were half-existent and half-non-existent prior, for these three cases to arise simultaneously is not possible.
Why is this? If seeing and knowing existed beforehand, they should not arise again, because they already exist.
If they did not exist beforehand, they likewise should not arise, because they do not exist.
If it were non-existent, there would be no mutual dependence and no arising.
If it were both existent and non-existent, this is already refuted by the two preceding sūtras respectively.
Furthermore, how can a single phenomenon both exist and not exist?
Furthermore, if they were to arise simultaneously, one would know without depending on seeing, and one would see without depending on knowing.
Furthermore, does the eye see by reaching the object?
Is it that one sees form without reaching it?
If the eye were to go out [to the object], then the *sūtra* would be seen only after a long delay.
If the eye must reach the form before seeing it, then distant forms should be seen slowly and near forms should be seen quickly.
Why is this? Because it is the nature of the faculty of sight not to travel.

Yet, one perceives both the nearby jar and the distant moon at the same time; therefore, we know that the eye does not go forth. If it did not go forth, there would be no conjunction [with the object].
Furthermore, if the eye perceives forms without its power reaching them, why does it see what is near but not what is far?
Near and far objects should be seen simultaneously.
Furthermore, if the eye were to go forth, would it see after having already gone?
Is it because one has not seen [the object] that one goes?
If one has already seen it, what further use is there for going?
If the eye has already seen the form and the matter is already accomplished, what further use is there for going?
If one does not see, one departs from the *sūtra* as it was intended to be grasped.
If the eye first does not see a form and then departs, one cannot grasp it as it was intended to be grasped; because the eye lacks cognition, if one intends to go east, one goes west.
Furthermore, one who lacks the sense-base of the eye does not grasp at the sūtras.
If the eye were to go to the form and grasp it, then the body would be without the eye.
Because the body would lack the eye, there would be no grasping.
If the eye were to apprehend form without going forth, then form would exist without the eye.
Since form would lack the eye, there would likewise be no apprehension of it.
Furthermore, if the eye were to apprehend form without going forth, one should be able to see forms in the heavens as well as forms obstructed by barriers.
However, since it is not seen, this matter is incorrect.
The opponent says:
"Because the characteristic of the eye sees, it is a Sūtra."
To see this characteristic of the eye is to have the power to apprehend within its conditions, for such is its inherent nature.
The internal [opponent] says:
If the eye sees by means of its own characteristic, it would follow that the *sūtra* states the eye sees itself.

If the eye were a faculty of seeing, it would be like the characteristic of fire’s heat, which, being hot by nature, can cause others to be hot; likewise, if the eye were a faculty of seeing, it should see itself.
Yet it does not see itself; therefore, the eye is not a faculty of seeing.
The opponent says:
It is like a finger pointing to a sūtra;
although the eye perceives forms, it does not perceive itself.
Just as the tip of a finger cannot touch itself, so too the eye, though it perceives objects, cannot see itself.
The internal [proponent] says: Not so.
"Contact" (spraṣṭavya) refers to the function (karman), as in the term *sūtra*;
contact is the function, not the characteristic (lakṣaṇa).
As for your statement that "seeing is the characteristic of the eye," why then does the eye not see itself?
Therefore, the analogy of the finger is incorrect.
The opponent says:
"The Sūtra states that because the faculty of sight goes out, it perceives form."
Because the visual faculty and the mind go forth, they are able to apprehend form upon reaching it.
The internal [opponent] says:
If the mind goes to the form, this contradicts the *Sūtra* which states that [the mind] is without sensation (*acetana*).
If the mind were to go to form, the mind would then be located there.
If the mind were located there, the body would be devoid of mind, like a dead person.
Yet, in reality, the mind does not go, because it perceives both the distant and the near simultaneously.
Although one recollects the past and the future, the recollection does not reside in the past or the future, because at the time of recollecting, [the mind] does not go [there].
The opponent says:
"The intention (manas) resides in the body; this is from the Sūtra."
"Although the mind resides within the body, it is able to know things at a distance.
The internal [opponent] says:
"If that were so, it would not accord with the Sūtras."
If the mind is in the body while the form is elsewhere, then because the form is elsewhere, there is no conjunction; if there is no conjunction, one cannot perceive the form.
The opponent says: Not so.
Because the mind, light, and form unite, one sees the sūtras.
When the eye and the mind are in harmony within the body, the power of the mind causes the light of the eyes to unite with form; thus one perceives form, and therefore the conjunction is not lost.
The internal [opponent] says: If seeing arises due to a combination, there is no "seer" in the sūtras.
You claim that seeing occurs through a combination; however, if you say that the eye alone sees form or the mind alone apprehends form, this is not the case.
The opponent says:
Because you accept a combination, the Sūtra is established by taking up form.
If you accept a combination, then there is a combination.
If there were a conjunction [of these factors], there would have to be the grasping of form.
The internal [proponent] says:
The mind does not see, the eye does not know, and form is neither seen nor known; how then can one see the Sūtra?
Because the mind is distinct from the eye, the mind does not possess the characteristic of seeing.
Since it lacks the characteristic of seeing, it cannot see the eye.
Furthermore, because it is composed of the four great elements, it does not possess the characteristic of cognition.
Because it does not have the characteristic of knowing, it cannot know form; nor does it have the characteristic of seeing, nor the characteristic of knowing.
Thus, although they are combined, how can form be grasped?
The ear, nose, tongue, and body are likewise refuted in this manner.
Chapter Six: Refuting the Objects of Perception (*Viṣayabhanga*). The opponent says:
According to the Sūtra, sentient beings, jars, and so forth must exist, because they are objects of perception (*grāhya*).
Since we currently perceive objects such as jars and the like as being graspable,
if the various sense faculties were unable to grasp their respective objects, by what means would they be grasped?
Therefore, we know that sentient beings are able to grasp objects such as jars and the like.
The internal [opponent] says:
It is not that form alone is the jar; therefore, the jar is not something perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) according to the Sūtra.
While the form within the jar is visible, its odor and other qualities are not.
It is not that form alone constitutes the jar; rather, the combination of fragrance and other qualities constitutes the jar.
If the jar were something perceptible to the senses, then fragrance and the others should also be perceptible.
Yet they are not so perceived; therefore, the jar is not perceptible.
The opponent says:
Because it grasps a portion [of the whole], it is "all-grasping" (*sarvagrāhin*); because it inspires confidence, it is a *sūtra*.
Since one part of a jar is visible, the jar is called "perceptible."
Why is this? Because when a person has seen a jar, they believe and know, "I have seen this jar.
The internal [opponent] says:
If one takes a portion, one does not take the entire *sūtra*.

For example, while the color-portion (*rūpa-bhāga*) of a jar is visible, its fragrance-portion (*gandha-bhāga*) and so forth are invisible; thus, the portion does not constitute the whole (*avayavin*).
If it were divided into parts, then the various parts such as fragrance and so forth would also be visible.
Therefore, the jar is not entirely visible; this matter has been explained in the refutation of oneness and difference.
The opponent says:
A jar exists and is visible, because the perception of color is visibly perceived; this is the Sūtra.
Since you accept that the perception of color is visibly perceived, the jar must also be visibly perceived.
The internal [opponent] says:
If this part is perceived through direct observation while that part is not perceived, then your *sūtra* is undermined.
You claim that form (*rūpa*) is perceived through direct observation; this is not so, because form possesses shape (*saṃsthāna*).
That part is not perceived as a distinct part because it is obstructed by this part; the same applies to that part as well.
Furthermore, if—as previously stated—one does not grasp all parts when collecting them, one should answer this accordingly.
The opponent says:
Since atoms have no parts, the *sūtras* are not entirely refuted.
Since atoms have no parts, what fault is there in everything being perceived as such?
The internal [opponent] says:
"The *sūtra* states that atoms are not perceptible.
Your scripture says that atoms are not perceptible; therefore, they cannot establish a perceptible phenomenon."
If atoms were also directly perceived, they would be refuted in the same manner as form (*rūpa*).
The opponent says:
A jar ought to be directly perceived, because the world trusts the *sūtra*.
The world universally believes that the jar is perceived through direct perception because it has utility.
The internal [proponent] says:
Direct perception does not exist; it is not the case that the *sūtra* on the non-existence of the jar is absent.
If you claim that when a jar is not perceived by direct observation, at that time the jar does not exist, this is not the case.
Although the jar is not manifest, its non-existence is not perceived; therefore, the jar is not something established through direct observation.
The opponent says:
There is no fault in the Sūtra because of the conjunction with the eye.
Although the jar possesses manifest characteristics, when it has not yet met with the eye, a person simply does not see it; it is not that its manifest characteristics do not exist.
The internal [opponent] says:
As it is directly perceived that arising is non-existent, so too existence is not truly established in the *sūtra*.

If, when a jar has not yet come into contact with the eye, there were no distinct characteristic (*viśeṣa*), and later, upon seeing it, some slight distinct characteristic were to arise, one should know that this jar is produced through the appearance of a directly perceived characteristic.
Now, in reality, no distinct characteristic arises; therefore, it is observed that characteristics do not arise.
Just as the arising of observed characteristics is non-existent, so too is the existence of the jar non-existent.
The opponent says:
If one part of the five constituents [of a pot] is destroyed, the remaining parts still possess the *sūtra* (the treatise).
These five constituents constitute the pot; you have destroyed one constituent, namely color (*rūpa*), but you have not destroyed fragrance (*gandha*) and the others.
Since fragrance and the others are not destroyed, there must therefore be atoms (*paramāṇu*).
The internal [opponent] says:
If not everything is touched, how can the *sūtra* speak of the conjunction of form and so forth?
You state that the five aggregates constitute a jar.
This statement is not correct.
Why? Because a portion of form and so forth is tangible, while other portions are not tangible; how, then, could the tangible and the intangible be conjoined?
Therefore, the five aggregates are not the jar.
The opponent says:
"The jar exists because it is a combination; this is the Sūtra."
The constituent parts of form and so forth do not individually combine, yet the constituent parts of form and so forth combine with the jar.
The internal [opponent] says:
If they are distinct, how can it be said that the jar combines with contact? This is from the Sūtra.
If the jar were different from its tangibility, then the jar would not be tangible; and how could that which is not tangible be conjoined with tangibility?
If, apart from color and so forth, there is no further dharma of "jar," then in the absence of such a dharma of "jar," how could tangibility be conjoined with the jar?
The opponent says:
Form should be directly perceived; this is because you accept the Sūtras as authoritative.
Your Sūtra states that form consists of the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements.
Among the derived forms (*upādāya-rūpa*), that which is subsumed under the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) is perceptible; how then can you say that perceptible form does not exist?
The internal [opponent] says:
The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are not seen by the eye; how then can they give rise to a perceptible *sūtra*?

The earth has the characteristic of solidity, water the characteristic of moisture, fire the characteristic of heat, and wind the characteristic of motion; if these four great elements are not visible to the eye, then the derived matter produced from them should likewise not be perceptible to the eye.
The opponent says:
Because they are apprehended by the faculty of the body, there are sūtras concerning the four great elements.
Now, because the four great elements are apprehended by the faculty of the body, the four great elements exist.
Therefore, objects such as fire, being composed of the four great elements, must also exist.
The internal [opponent] says:
"Because all that is within fire is hot; thus it is stated in the Sūtra."
Among the four great elements, only fire has the characteristic of heat, while the others do not.
Now, within fire, all four great elements possess the characteristic of heat; therefore, fire does not constitute a body of four [elements].
If that which is not hot were not called fire, then fire would not constitute one of the four bodies.
It is the same for earth, whose characteristic is solidity; water, whose characteristic is moisture; and wind, whose characteristic is motion.
The opponent says:
Form should be visible, because it exists at the present time, as stated in the Sūtras.
Since the sense-faculties such as the eye apprehend objects at the present time, this is called "the present time."
If the visual faculty and so forth were unable to apprehend visible objects and so forth, then there would be no present time.
Since present time truly exists, visible objects can therefore be seen.
The internal [opponent] says:
If a dharma is old later, it must also have been old at the beginning; this is the Sūtra.

If a dharma manifests its marks as being old later, these marks do not arise at the time when they were old; rather, they already existed following [the dharma] at the moment of its initial arising. Because they were subtle and unknown, the marks manifested later, at which time they became knowable.
It is like a person wearing wooden clogs; because they are initially worn thin, one follows along with them without realizing or knowing it, yet after a long time, the signs become manifest.
If there were no wear at the beginning, there would be none at the end either, and thus they would remain perpetually new.
If this were the case, then characteristics (lakṣaṇa) should not arise.
Therefore, because they are initially subtle, one follows them; subsequently, the characteristics manifest.
Now, because all phenomena do not abide, there is no time of abiding; if there is no time of abiding, there is no locus for grasping objects.
The opponent says:
Because you accept the new and the old, there exists the present time; this is stated in the Sūtra.
You accept both the characteristic of the new and the characteristic of the old.

Observing it at the time of arising is called "new," and observing it at the time of change is called "old. These two characteristics cannot be apprehended in the past, nor can they be apprehended in the future.
Because it exists in the present time, the characteristics of the new and the old can be apprehended.
The internal [opponent] says: Not so.
Because it has arisen, it is "new"; because it has changed, it is "old," O Sūtra.

If a dharma has long since arisen and its characteristic of newness has already passed, this change from the characteristic of newness is called "old. If the characteristic of oldness arises, then it becomes "new. This "new" and "old" exist only as verbal designations; in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no new, no middle, and no old.
The outsider asks:
"If that is so, what benefit is gained?
The insider replies:
One attains permanent detachment from the *sūtras*.

If the new does not become the middle, and the middle does not become the old—just as the seed, sprout, stalk, node, flower, fruit, and so forth do not coalesce—because they do not coalesce, all phenomena do not abide; because they do not abide, they are detached; and because they are detached, they cannot be grasped.
7. Refuting the Theory that the Effect Exists within the Cause. Chapter Seven. The opponent says:
"All phenomena do not fail to abide, because that which exists is not lost and that which does not exist is not produced; so it is stated in the Sūtra."
All phenomena possessing characteristics are like a lump of clay; from its base, from its belly, from its throat, and from its mouth, the preceding and succeeding parts function as cause and effect.
When various effects arise, their various causes are not lost.
If the effect were not present within the cause, the effect would not arise.
Rather, it is because the cause transforms into the effect that all phenomena exist.
The internal [opponent] says:

If it is because an effect arises that there is no loss, then according to the *sūtra* on "loss through the loss of the cause," when the jar as an effect arises, the lump of clay is not lost; thus, the jar is identical to the lump of clay.
If the effect, the jar, were to arise, at that time the cause, the lump of clay, would have perished; thus, it would be without a cause.
If the lump of clay did not perish, one could not distinguish between the lump of clay and the jar as being different.
Now, since we actually observe differences in form, time, power, cognition, name, and so forth, there must be something that perishes.
The opponent says:
It is like the Sūtra on the bending and stretching of a finger.
Although the finger changes form when bent or extended, it remains in reality one and the same finger.
Likewise, although the lump of clay and the form of the jar differ, the clay itself does not differ.
The internal [opponent] says:
Not so; because karma can produce differentiation, it is called *sūtra*.
"Bending and extending" refers to karma, while the "finger" refers to the capacity [of that karma].
If the action were identical to the agent, then when the finger bends, it should be lost; furthermore, bending and extending would have to be one and the same.
According to your own scripture, since the lump of clay is identical to the jar, your analogy of the finger is incorrect.
The opponent says:
It is as in the *Sūtra* on youth, adulthood, and old age.
Just as a single person’s body is both young, adult, and old, so too are cause and effect.
The internal [opponent] says:
Because things are not identical, there is no *sūtra* [that supports your claim].
That which is young does not become old, and that which is old does not become young; therefore, your analogy is incorrect.
Furthermore, if there were non-perishing (*avipraṇāśa*), there would be no sūtra on perishing.
If there were non-perishing, a lump of clay should not transform into a jar; in that case, there would be no jar.
If there were no non-loss, then because non-existence would not exist, there should likewise be no loss; thus, there would be no loss at all.
The opponent says:
What fault is there in the Sūtra [stating] that there is no loss?
If [the lump of clay] remains constant and thus undergoes no change, then the lump of clay should not transform into a jar.
What fault is there in the absence of impermanence?
The internal [opponent] says:
If there were no impermanence, there would be no *sūtras* concerning demerit, merit, and so forth.
If there were no impermanence, demerit, merit, and all such things would likewise not exist. Why is this?
A sinner always acts as a sinner and should not perform meritorious deeds;
a person of merit always acts as one of merit and should not commit sins.

For those for whom sin and merit are equal, there would likewise be no such distinctions as giving versus stealing, or observing versus violating the precepts. Thus, all such things would be non-existent.
The opponent says:
The effect exists prior to the cause; because the cause exists, there is the sūtra.
If the jar did not exist prior to the clay, the clay would not be the cause of the jar.
The internal [opponent] says:
If it is because the effect pre-exists that the cause exists, then according to the *sūtra*, since the effect is non-existent, the cause is without effect.
If a lump of clay is made into a jar, because the clay is not lost, the effect exists within the cause.
If this jar were to break, it would follow that the effect does not exist within the cause.
The opponent says:
According to the Sūtra, cause and effect are one.

Just as clay is the cause for the effect of a jar, and mud is the cause for the effect of a pot, there is no distinct phenomenon other than the cause transforming into the effect; therefore, it is not the case that the effect does not exist within the cause.
The internal [opponent] says:
If cause and effect were one and the same, there would be no future *sūtras*.

For example, when the lump of clay is present, the jar is future. If cause and effect were one and the same, there would be no future; because there is no future, there would also be no present; and because there is no present, there would also be no past. In this way, the three periods of time would become confused.
The opponent says:
Because names and so forth perish and names and so forth arise, there is a *sūtra* [that states this].
There are no new dharmas, nor do old dharmas perish; it is merely that names differ according to the occasion.
Just as a lump of clay becomes a jar, the jar breaks to become a basin, and the basin breaks back into clay;
in this way, there is ultimately no coming or going—where, then, do the jar and the basin abide?
"It is merely that they receive different names according to the occasion, but in reality there is no difference.
The internal [opponent] says:
"If that were so, then according to the Sūtra, there would be no cause for the fruit."

If it is claimed that the name perishes and a new name arises, then this name would have been non-existent previously and come into existence later; therefore, the effect would not exist within the cause.
If the name existed previously, then the clay would already be the jar.
Therefore, it is known that the effect does not pre-exist.
The opponent says:
This is because the *sūtra* is inconclusive.
Since a specific vessel is not predetermined within a lump of clay, the name "clay" is likewise not predetermined therein.
The internal [proponent] says:
If the clay is indeterminate, then the fruit is also indeterminate; this is a *sūtra*.
If the jar is not determinate within the lump of clay, then your statement that the effect pre-exists within the cause is also not determinate.
The opponent says:
"Because the subtle form exists, it is stated in the Sūtra."
Within a lump of clay, the form of a jar is subtle and thus difficult to perceive; however, through the power of the potter, it becomes clearly manifest at that time.
Although the jar cannot be known within the clay, one should understand that its subtle form must necessarily exist within the clay.
There are two kinds of unknowability:
either it is unknown because it does not exist, or it is unknown due to causes and conditions.
There are eight such causes and conditions.
What are the eight?
One does not know because of distance, as with a distant land.
One does not know because of proximity, as with one's own eyelashes.
One does not know because the faculties are impaired, as in the case of the deaf and blind;
one does not know because the mind does not abide, as in the case of a person whose mind is distracted;
and one does not know because [the object] is subtle, as in the case of a minute particle of dust.
One does not know due to obstruction, as with objects beyond a wall;
one does not know due to being overwhelmed, as when a small amount of salt is placed in a great body of water;
and one does not know due to similarity, as when a single grain of rice is thrown into a large heap.
In this way, although the jar within the lump of clay is not seen by the eye, it certainly does not emerge from the *tūla* grass; therefore, the subtle jar must definitely exist within the clay.
The internal [opponent] says:
If the subtle form existed beforehand, it would contradict the *sūtra* which states that the effect does not exist in the cause.

If it is argued that when the jar has not yet arisen, its subtle form exists within the clay and can be known later at the time of its gross manifestation, then this implies that the effect does not exist within the cause. Why is this so?
Because that which was originally without coarse characteristics subsequently arises, for this reason there is no effect within the cause.
The opponent says:
There must be an effect within the cause, because the sūtras state that one takes up each respective cause.
The effect must already exist within the cause.
Why? Because when making a jar, one takes clay and does not take reeds.
If the effect were not present within the cause, one might as well take reeds [to make a jar].
Yet people know for certain that clay can produce a jar; because it is kneaded into a vessel and is capable of withstanding firing, the effect must exist within the cause.
The internal [opponent] says:
If there were existence where there ought to be existence, or non-existence where there ought to be non-existence,
then according to your sūtra which states that a jar shall emerge from within the clay, the effect must pre-exist within the cause.
Now, because the jar has been destroyed, there should be no effect; therefore, the effect does not exist within the cause.
The opponent says:
There is no fault, because the sequence of arising, abiding, and destruction exists in the Sūtra.
Although the jar possesses the characteristic of disintegration, it must first arise, then abide, and finally disintegrate.
Why is this? Because there is no disintegration prior to its arising.
The internal [opponent] says:
If that which arises first is not that which ceases later, there would be no result, as in the case of the *sūtra*.
If a jar were to arise within the clay and immediately perish, why must it necessarily arise first and perish later, rather than perishing first and arising later?

You say that because it has not yet arisen, there is no destruction; likewise, when a jar has not yet arisen, there is neither abiding nor destruction. Since these two [abiding and destruction] are non-existent beforehand and come into existence later, the effect does not exist within the cause.
The opponent says:
"Because you refute the existence of an effect, there is the fault of nihilism (*uccheda-doṣa*) in your sūtra.
If it is incorrect that the effect exists within the cause, then the effect must not exist within the cause."
If the effect does not exist within the cause, one falls into the error of nihilism.
The internal [proponent] says:
Because there is continuity, it is not annihilated; because there is disintegration, it is not eternal—thus it is taught in the Sūtras.
Do you not know? Because there is a continuity from the grain seed through the sprout and so forth, it is not annihilated; because the causes such as the grain seed perish, it is not eternal.

Thus, the Buddhas teach the dharma of dependent origination in twelve links, which, by being free from the views that the effect exists within the cause or does not exist at all, avoids the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, and proceeds via the Middle Way into nirvana.
Chapter Eight: Refuting the Absence of the Effect within the Cause. The opponent says:
Because there is arising, one *sūtra* should be established.
You state that all phenomena arise by way of causes and conditions.
Is this arising pre-existent within the cause,
or is it non-existent within the cause?
Since this arising exists, there must necessarily be that [cause] which possesses it.
The internal [opponent] says:
Regarding the *sūtra* on "arising from non-arising" and "non-arising," if there is arising,
does it already exist within the cause?
Is it that [the jar] did not previously exist within the cause?
Such contemplation is untenable; how much more so the case of non-arising.
If you maintain that a jar arises, does it exist at the very first moment of being a jar?
Does it exist at a time subsequent to the lump of clay when it is no longer a jar?
If the jar were to arise while existing at its initial stage as a jar, that would not be possible. Why is this so?
Since the jar already exists, it is mutually dependent upon its beginning, middle, and end; if there were no middle or end, there would be no beginning.
If there is a beginning of the jar, there must necessarily be a middle and an end.
Therefore, since the jar already exists beforehand, what further use is there for its arising?
If it is argued that the jar arises at a time subsequent to the lump of clay when it is no longer a lump, this too is not tenable. Why?
Because it does not yet exist.
If a jar lacks a beginning, middle, and end, then there is no jar.
If there is no jar, how can there be the arising of a jar?
Furthermore, if a jar were to arise, would it exist at the time after the lump of clay,
or would it exist at the initial time of the lump of clay?
At the time after the lump of clay, there is no arising of a jar.
Why is this? Because it already exists.
Furthermore, the jar does not arise at the initial stage when it is still a lump of clay.
Why is this? Because it does not yet exist.
The opponent says:
The *sūtra* states: "There is no fault because it arises at the time of arising.
I do not say that there is the arising of a jar either when it has already arisen or when it has not yet arisen; rather, it is this second dharma that arises at the time of arising.
The internal [opponent] says:
The *sūtra* on the time of birth is also like this.
The time of birth is as previously explained.
If it has already arisen, then it is already arisen; if it has not yet arisen, how can there be arising?
The time of arising is called half-arisen and half-unarisen; both positions entail errors, as was already refuted previously.
Therefore, there is no arising.
The opponent says:
A sūtra is so called because "arising" (utpāda) and "generation" (janman) have the same meaning.
I do not say that the jar has already arisen when it arises, nor do I say that there is arising for that which has not yet arisen;
rather, the jar is now manifestly accomplished, and this is precisely the arising of the jar.
The internal [opponent] says:
If that is so, after the arising of the sūtra,
it is designated as "already arisen.
If there were no arising, there would be neither beginning nor middle.
If there is no beginning, there is also no middle and no completion.
Therefore, one should not regard completion as arising, because arising occurs later.
The opponent says:
There is no fault in the *sūtra* because things arise in a sequence of beginning, middle, and end.

Just as a lump of clay arises sequentially as the base, belly, neck, and mouth of a jar—arising in a sequence of beginning, middle, and end—it is not that the jar is formed immediately following the lump of clay.
Therefore, it is not the case that a jar arises while it is still a lump of clay; nor does a jar arise at the time of the jar itself; nor does it arise without being a jar.
The internal [proponent] says:
The *sūtra* states that there is no sequential arising of beginning, middle, and end.
The first is called "having no prior but having a posterior"; the middle is called "having both a prior and a posterior"; and the last is called "having a prior but no posterior.
Thus, beginning, middle, and end exist in mutual dependence; if they were separated, how could they exist?
Therefore, the beginning, middle, and end should not arise sequentially;
nor is it correct for them to arise simultaneously, as stated in the Sūtra.
If they were to arise simultaneously, one could not say "this is the beginning," "this is the middle," or "this is the end," and they would not be mutually dependent; therefore, this is not the case.
The opponent says:
It is as in the *sūtra* on arising, abiding, and destruction.
Just as the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*) exist in the sequence of arising, abiding, and destruction, so too are there the beginning, middle, and end.
The internal [opponent] says:
The Sūtra also states that arising, abiding, and destruction are likewise sequential.
If they exist in such a sequence?
If they were to exist simultaneously,
these two cases would not be possible. Why is this?
Where there is no abiding, there is no arising.
If there were arising without abiding, then there would likewise be abiding without arising; the same applies to destruction.
If these were simultaneous, one should not differentiate between this being arising, this being abiding, and this being destruction.
Furthermore, in every instance there is the entire *sūtra*.

"Every instance" refers to the three characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*). If birth, abiding, and destruction were themselves characteristics of the conditioned, then within the present [moment] there would have to be three characteristics, because it is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Within each of these, there would again be three characteristics, and thus they would be infinite.
The same applies to abiding and destruction.
If within arising, abiding, and destruction there were no further three characteristics, then arising, abiding, and destruction could not be called the characteristics of the conditioned.
If you claim that "arising" and "the arising of arising" arise together like father and son, this is not so. In this case,
regarding the arising of arising, does it first exist in dependence within the cause,
or does it first not exist in dependence within the cause?
If there were a prior existence, even slight or minimal, of mutual dependence within the cause, these three types of refutations have already been explained.
Furthermore, it is like a father who exists first and only then gives birth to a son; if that father must himself have another father, this analogy is therefore invalid.
The opponent says:
There must be production and that which is produced, because the *dharmas* exist; for there is a *sūtra* [stating] that if there is production, there is that which is produced.
If there were no arising, then nothing could arise.
Now, since phenomena such as jars that are subject to arising are currently evident, arising must necessarily exist.
The internal [opponent] says:
If there is arising, there is no "arising-able" (*utpādya*) *sūtra*.
If a jar has arisen, the jar has already arisen and is not called "arising-able. Why is this?
If there is no jar, there is also no arising of a jar.
Therefore, if there is arising, there is nothing that can arise; how much more so in the case of non-arising?
Furthermore, the sūtra explains that the same applies to [arising] from self, from another, or from both.
If "arising" and "that which arises" are these two, whether they arise from themselves, from another, or from both, this has already been refuted in the *Vigraha-vyāvartanī*.
The opponent says:
"Arising must certainly exist because arising and that which arises are established together; thus it is stated in the Sūtra."
That which has already arisen cannot give rise to that which is yet to arise; they cannot be established simultaneously.
The internal [opponent] says:
The "arising" (utpāda) cannot give rise to the "arising-to-be-arisen" (janyotpāda); this is a sūtra.
If that which is capable of producing could itself be produced, then "production" would be something that is produced and could not be called "the producer.
If there is no production, how can there be that which is produced?
Therefore, both of these things are non-existent.
Furthermore, it is not the case that existence and non-existence are mutually dependent, as stated in the Sūtra.
Since that which is yet to arise must first be non-existent, non-arising is itself existence; how, then, can existence and non-existence be mutually dependent?
Therefore, all things are non-existent.
The opponent says:
Because "arising" and "that which arises" exist in mutual dependence, all dharmas are established; this is the Sūtra.
It is not only that "arising" and "that which arises" are established through mutual dependence; because these two depend upon each other, all things such as jars are established.
The internal [opponent] says: If they arise from two, why is there no third *sūtra*?
You say that because arising and that which arises are mutually dependent, all phenomena are established.
If a fruit were produced from two [factors], why would there not be a third factor, just as when parents give birth to a child?
Now, since that which has arisen is already separated from that which is yet to arise, there is no third dharma such as a jar; therefore, this is not the case.
The opponent says:
There must be arising, because the Sūtra states, "due to the destruction of the cause."
If the effect were not to arise, the cause should not perish.
Now, since we observe that the cause of the jar perishes, there must be an arising.
The internal [proponent] says:
The *sūtra* states: "Because of the destruction of the cause, the arising [of the effect] also ceases.
If an effect were to arise, would that effect exist at the time the cause is being destroyed, or would it exist after the cause has been destroyed?
If [the effect] exists at the time the cause perishes, it would not be distinct from the perishing; therefore, arising would also be cessation.
If [the effect] exists after the cause has perished, then because the cause has already ceased, there would be no cause; and since there is no cause, the effect should not arise.
Furthermore, because the effect is determinate within the cause, it is called *sūtra*.
If the effect already exists within the cause, or if it does not exist within the cause—both cases are equally without production. Why is this so?
If the effect were not present within the cause, why would there be a jar only in the clay and cloth only in the threads?
If both were equally non-existent [in their respective causes], then the clay should contain the cloth and the threads should contain the jar.
If the effect already existed within the cause, then that effect would arise from within the cause. This is not so. Why?
The cause is itself the effect, because in your doctrine the cause and effect are not distinct.
Therefore, whether the effect pre-exists within the cause or does not pre-exist, it is in neither case produced.
Furthermore, it is called *sūtra* because causes and effects are manifold.
If the effect were already present within the cause, then curd and butter would exist within milk, and likewise, curd and milk would exist within butter.
If curd, butter, and so forth were already present within milk, then there would be many effects from a single cause.
If curd, milk, and so forth were already present within butter, then there would be many causes within a single effect.
In this way, there is the fault that cause and effect would exist simultaneously,
whether the effect is considered to be present within the cause or not. Therefore,
whether the effect exists within the cause or does not exist within it, in both cases there is no arising.
The opponent says:
Since cause and effect are not refuted, the *sūtra* stating that "arising arises" is valid.

Your objection—that it is a fault for there to be many effects within a cause or many causes within an effect—does not claim that cause and effect do not exist; therefore, "arising arises" is tenable.
The internal [proponent] says:
"Each thing is not a thing; things and non-things do not mutually produce one another, as stated in the Sūtra.
A thing does not produce a thing, a non-thing does not produce a non-thing, a thing does not produce a non-thing, and a non-thing does not produce a thing."
If a thing were to produce another thing, as a mother gives birth to a son, this would not be so.
Why? Because a mother does not actually give birth to a son.
The child already exists [in potential], for it emerges from the mother.
If you claim that it is produced as a physical entity from the maternal blood-stream, this is also not so. Why is this?
Because a mother distinct from the blood-element and so forth cannot be found.
If it is argued that, like a transformation-born being, [the mother] acts as the producer of the entity, this is also not the case. Why?
Youth transforms into old age; it is not that youth gives birth to old age.
If you claim that it is like a reflection in a mirror, which produces the object, this too is not so.
Why is this? Because the reflection in a mirror comes from nowhere.
Furthermore, just as a reflection in a mirror resembles the face, other effects should likewise resemble their causes.
But this is not the case; therefore, an entity does not produce a non-entity.
That a non-entity does not produce a non-entity is like a rabbit’s horn not producing a rabbit’s horn.
That an entity does not produce a non-entity is like a barren woman not giving birth to a child.
That which is not a thing does not produce things, just as the hair of a tortoise does not produce *pú* grass.
Therefore, there is no phenomenon that arises.
Furthermore, if a thing were to produce a thing, it would have to arise through two kinds of phenomena:
Whether the effect exists within the cause or does not exist within the cause,
neither is tenable. Why is this so?
If the effect does not pre-exist within the cause, the cause should not produce the effect, because a result distinct from the cause cannot be found at the side of the cause.
If the effect already pre-exists within the cause, how can there be arising and ceasing?
It is called *sūtra* because it is not different [from its cause].
If the jar were not different from the lump of clay, then when the jar arises, the lump of clay should not cease; furthermore, the lump of clay would not be the cause of the jar.
If the lump of clay were not different from the jar, the jar would not arise as a jar, nor could it be the effect of the lump of clay.
Therefore, whether the effect exists within the cause or does not exist within the cause, an entity does not produce an entity.
Chapter Nine: Refuting the Permanent. The Outsider says:
There must exist dharmas that are permanent and without cause, for the Sūtra does not refute them.
Although you have refuted dharmas that possess causes, you have not refuted permanent dharmas that lack causes.
Just as space, time, direction, atoms, and nirvāṇa are causeless phenomena (*ahetuka-dharma*), so too should all phenomena exist, for they cannot be destroyed.
The internal [opponent] says:
If one forcibly asserts that these are permanent, then impermanence is likewise established by the Sūtras (*sūtra*).
Do you assert that [things] are eternal because they have a cause,
or do you assert that they are eternal because they lack a cause?
If an eternal dharma has a cause, then having a cause implies it is impermanent.
If one asserts that something is eternal because it lacks a cause, then one might as well assert that it is impermanent.
The opponent says:
There is no fault in this *sūtra*, because it refers to a "revealing cause" (*vyañjanahetu*).
There are two kinds of causes:
first, the producing cause; second, the revealing cause.
If it were by way of a producing cause, then it would be impermanent.

My dharmas, such as space and so forth, are said to be eternal because they are characterized by the cause of manifestation; they are not said to be eternal due to a lack of cause, nor are they said to be impermanent due to having a cause. Therefore, it is not that I am arbitrarily asserting them to be eternal.
The internal [opponent] says:
This reason is not valid according to the Sūtras.
Although you claim that eternal dharmas have a cause, this reason is invalid; the self (*ātman*) has already been refuted, and the remaining eternal dharmas shall be refuted later.
The opponent says:
There must exist eternal dharmas, because created dharmas are impermanent; therefore, according to the Sūtra, uncreated dharmas are eternal.
We see with our own eyes that objects such as jars are impermanent; if there were a dharma different from these, it would have to be eternal.
The internal [opponent] says:
There are also *sūtras* that speak of non-existence being common [to both].

You claim it is "non-action" (*akriyā*) because it contradicts the characteristics of action (*kriyā-dharma*); however, since we now observe that characteristics exist within action, there should be no such thing as "non-action."

Furthermore, if you maintain that because it contradicts the nature of being produced (*kṛtaka*), the unproduced is eternal, then since it does not contradict the nature of being produced now, it ought to be impermanent. Why is this so?
Since non-action and action are equally devoid of contact, non-action would have to be impermanent.
In this way, both the universal permanence and the non-universal permanence of all things are comprehensively refuted.
Now, this shall be refuted separately.
The opponent says:
Space as a dharma definitely exists, is eternal, all-pervading, and partless; for it is taught in the Sūtras that it is to be believed to exist in all places and at all times.
Ordinary people believe that space exists in all places; therefore, they universally believe that space exists at all times—past, future, and present—and for this reason, it is eternal.
The internal [opponent] says:
Because parts are combined within parts, parts are not different from the *sūtra*.
If there is empty space within a jar or within a bowl, is that empty space a totality?
Is it [space] that exists as a portion?
If it exists as a whole, then it would not be pervasive.
If it were pervasive in this way, then the jar should also be pervasive.
If it possesses parts, then space would consist merely of the absence of parts.
Since that which possesses parts is called "space," therefore space is neither all-pervasive nor eternal.
The opponent says:
Space certainly exists; its pervasive characteristic is also eternal, for there is a sūtra stating that it is produced.
If space did not exist, then there would be no lifting up or lowering down, nor going and coming, and so forth.
Why is this so? Because there is no place where it could be contained.
Now, since there is indeed that which is made, there must therefore be space, which is both pervasive and eternal.
The internal [opponent] says: Not so.
It is stated in the *Ākāśānantyāyatana-sūtra*: "Space abides in space."
If there were such a thing as space, it would have to have a place of abiding.
If there were no place of abiding, then it would not be a real phenomenon.
If it were to abide within the cavities of space, then that place of abiding for space would itself be within space, because space possesses the capacity to contain.
But this is not so; therefore, space does not abide within cavities, nor does it abide within solid substances. Why is this?
Because there is truly no emptiness, it is called a sūtra;
this reality is not named "emptiness.
If there were no emptiness, there would be no place of abiding, because there would be no space for reception.

Furthermore, regarding your statement that space is the locus of activity: since there is no locus of activity within reality, space does not exist; therefore, space is neither omnipresent nor eternal.

Furthermore, because it lacks characteristics (*animitta*), space does not exist. All phenomena each possess their own characteristic; because they possess characteristics, one knows that phenomena exist—such as the characteristic of solidity for earth, moisture for water, heat for fire, motion for wind, and cognition for consciousness. Space, however, has no characteristic; therefore, it does not exist.
The opponent says:
Space possesses characteristics; it is nonexistent only because you do not recognize them.
The absence of form is the characteristic of space.
The internal [opponent] says: Not so.
The term "formless" (ārūpya) means the destruction of form; it does not imply the existence of some further dharma.
It is like a felled tree; there is no further dharma.
Therefore, there is no characteristic of space.
Furthermore, space is without characteristics.
Why is this? If you say that the absence of form (*rūpa*) is the characteristic of space (*ākāśa*), then at the time when form has not yet arisen, there would be no characteristic of space.

Furthermore, form is an impermanent phenomenon (*anityadharma*), whereas space is an eternal phenomenon (*nityadharma*); therefore, when form does not yet exist, the phenomenon of space should already exist beforehand.
If there were no form that could be extinguished, space would have no characteristic; if it had no characteristic, it would not be a dharma.
Therefore, it is not the absence of form that constitutes the characteristic of space; it is merely a name without reality.
All pervasive and eternal [entities] are likewise refuted in general.
The opponent says:
There exists a phenomenon at a certain time, because the characteristic of permanence exists; this is the Sūtra.
There are phenomena that, although not directly perceptible, are believed to exist because they are known through their common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Likewise, although time is subtle and invisible, one knows that time exists by means of seasonal changes, flowers, fruits, and so forth; this is knowing the cause by seeing the effect.
Furthermore, because of such characteristics as simultaneity and non-simultaneity, as well as duration and proximity, one can know that time exists.
There is no state where time does not exist; therefore, it is eternal.
The internal [opponent] says:
Since it does not exist within the past or the future, there is no future *sūtra*.

For example, when it is a lump of clay, it is present; when it is earth, it is past; and when it is a jar, it is future. Because these temporal characteristics (*kālalakṣaṇa*) are constant, the past time does not become the future time.
Your sūtra states that time is a single dharma; therefore, past time never becomes future time, nor does it become present time.
If past time were to become future time, there would be the fault of confusion.
Furthermore, within the past there is no time of the future; therefore, the future does not exist.
The present is likewise refuted in this manner.
The opponent says:
Because you accept the existence of past time, there are sūtras [that teach it].
Since you accept the existence of past time, there must necessarily be future time; therefore, time as a real dharma exists.
The internal [opponent] says:
It is not the case that the past *sūtra* possesses future characteristics.
Have you not heard what I previously stated: that past clay does not constitute a future jar?
If it falls within the characteristic of the future, it is the characteristic of the future; how then could it be called the past?
Therefore, the past does not exist.
The opponent says:
There must be time (*kāla*), because of the distinction between their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
If the present possesses the characteristic of the present, the past possesses the characteristic of the past, and the future possesses the characteristic of the future, therefore time exists.
The internal [opponent] says:
If that were so, then all *sūtras* currently existing—
if they possessed their own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) across the three times— should now all be present.
If it were future, it would be non-existent.
If it were existent, it could not be called "future"; it should instead be called "already come.
Therefore, this interpretation is incorrect.
The opponent says:
There is no fault in the Sūtra because past and future formations possess their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
At the time of the past and at the time of the future, they do not function with the characteristics of the present.

The past functions with the characteristic of the past, and the future functions with the characteristic of the future; since each functions according to its own specific characteristic, there is no fault.
The internal [opponent] says:
"The *sūtra* states that the past is not the past."
If that which has passed were itself past, it could not be called "the past.
Why? Because it would be devoid of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Just as fire, if it were to abandon its heat, would no longer be called fire because it would be devoid of its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);
likewise, if the past were not past, one should not now say that formations of the past possess the characteristics of the past.
The future is likewise refuted in this manner.
Therefore, the phenomenon of time lacks substantial reality and exists as mere verbal designation.
The opponent says:
Direction truly exists because the characteristic of permanence exists; this is the *sūtra*.
The point where the sun first meets [the horizon] is the characteristic of direction.
As stated in my sūtras: whether past, future, or present, the place where the sun first meets [the horizon] is called the eastern direction.
In this way, the names of the other directions follow the movement of the sun.
An internal objection states: Not so.
Because the east has no beginning, it is called *sūtra*.
The sun travels across the four continents, circling Mount Sumeru; when it is midday in Uttarakuru, the sun rises in Pūrvavideha, and the people of Pūrvavideha consider that to be the east.
When it is midday in Pūrvavideha, the sun rises in Jambudvīpa; the people of Jambudvīpa consider that to be the east.
When it is midday in Jambudvīpa, the sun rises in Aparagoyānī; the people of Aparagoyānī consider that to be the east.
When it is midday in Godānīya, it is sunrise in Uttarakuru; the people of Uttarakuru consider that to be the east.
In this way, all directions—east, south, west, and north—are established.
Furthermore, that which is called a non-directional point has no fixed orientation, because it is without characteristics (*animitta*).
Moreover, because it is indeterminate—such that what one person considers the east, another may consider the west—therefore, there is no real direction.
The opponent says:
Not so. This is a *sūtra* because it explains the characteristics of directions throughout the entire world.
This directional characteristic is explained with reference to a single world-system; it is not a universal statement. Therefore, the fault that the eastern direction has no beginning does not apply.
The internal [opponent] says:
If that were so, there would be a sūtra concerning finitude.

If that which first coincides with the sun were called the eastern direction, then all directions would have boundaries; because they have boundaries, they would have parts; and because they have parts, they would be impermanent.
Therefore, while it is said that there are directions, in reality, there are no directions.
The opponent says:
Although there is no all-pervasive permanence, there exist non-pervasive and impermanent atoms (*paramāṇu*), because the characteristics of an effect exist, as stated in the Sūtra.

People in the world sometimes know that a cause exists upon seeing an effect, or know that an effect exists upon seeing a cause; for example, by seeing a sprout and so forth, they know that a seed exists.

According to the worldly view of phenomena, one observes that all living beings are subtle at first and become coarse later; thus, it can be known that two atoms (*paramāṇu*) constitute the primary effect, having a single atom as their cause. Therefore, these atoms are spherical and eternal, for they lack a further cause.
The internal [opponent] says:
Two atoms do not combine with their entire bodies, because the resulting effect would not be spherical; this is the Sūtra.
When the effects of the various atoms arise, they do not combine with their entire bodies.
Why is this? Because the effects consisting of two atoms and so forth are not seen by the eye to be spherical.
If the bodies of the atoms were entirely joined together, then the effects consisting of two atoms and so forth would also have to be spherical.
Furthermore, if the entire body were to combine [with another], both would likewise perish.

If atoms were to combine part-for-part, the resulting effect would be higher; if many were to combine, the effect would be larger. Because they combine by way of one part, atoms must have parts; because they have parts, they are impermanent.
Furthermore, atoms are impermanent because they are distinct from space, as stated in the Sūtra.
If atoms existed, they would have to be distinct from space;
therefore, atoms possess parts, and because they possess parts, they are impermanent.
Furthermore, because of the distinctions such as color and taste, there is the *sūtra*.
If atoms were to exist, they would necessarily possess portions of color, taste, and so forth.
Therefore, atoms have parts; and because they have parts, they are impermanent.
Furthermore, conditioned phenomena possess characteristics because they have form.
If atoms possessed form, they would necessarily have dimensions such as length, shortness, squareness, or roundness; therefore, atoms must have parts. Because they have parts, they are impermanent.
Because it is impermanent, there are no atoms.
The opponent says:
There exists the dharma of nirvāṇa; it is eternal and free from afflictions, for the sūtra states that nirvāṇa is not different [from this].
The eternal exhaustion of all afflictions, such as craving and the like, is called nirvāṇa.
Those who possess afflictions undergo birth and death; because they lack afflictions, they never again undergo birth and death. Therefore, nirvāṇa is permanent.
The internal [proponent] says: Not so;
because *nirvāṇa* is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), it is a *sūtra*.

If, by virtue of practicing the path, one is free from all afflictions, and if being free from afflictions constitutes nirvana, then nirvana would be a conditioned phenomenon; and because it is a conditioned phenomenon, it would be impermanent.
Furthermore, if there were no afflictions, that would be called "nothingness.
If nirvāṇa were not distinct from the absence of afflictions, then there would be no nirvāṇa.
The opponent says:
Because it acts as a cause, it is a sūtra.
Nirvāṇa acts as the cause for the absence of afflictions.
The internal [opponent] says:
Not so. That which can destroy is not the destruction of the sūtras.
If nirvāṇa could act as liberation, then it would not be liberation.
Furthermore, as long as the afflictions have not been exhausted, there should be no nirvana. Why is this?
Because where there is no fruit, there is no cause.
The opponent says:
There is a sūtra stating that there is no fruit of the absence of afflictions.

This nirvāṇa is neither the absence of afflictions itself, nor is it the cause of the absence of afflictions; rather, it is the fruit of the absence of afflictions. Therefore, it is not the case that nirvāṇa does not exist.
The internal [proponent] says:
Bondage, that which is bound, and the means—apart from these, there is no use for the sūtras.
"Bondage" refers to afflictions and karma; "that which is bound" refers to sentient beings; and "the means" refers to the Eightfold Noble Path.
Because one is liberated from bondage by means of the Path, sentient beings attain liberation.
If there were a nirvāṇa distinct from these three dharmas, it would serve no purpose.
Furthermore, the absence of afflictions is called "non-existence," and non-existence should not function as a cause.
The outsider says:
There is nirvāṇa; otherwise, there would be no sūtras.
When these three things—the bound, that which can be bound, and the means—have no locus, this is called nirvāṇa.
The internal [opponent] says:
How can one be subject to defilement regarding what is a place of fear?
Because of the faults of impermanence, the wise abandon conditioned phenomena and become free from desire for them.
If nirvana is devoid of all sentient beings and objects of desire, then why is it that your mind is defiled by the fear of nirvana as being a place of great terror compared to conditioned phenomena?

Nirvana is named the departure from all attachments and the cessation of all conceptualizations; it is neither existent nor non-existent, neither a thing nor a non-thing, just as the extinguishing of a lamp cannot be described in words.
The outsider asks:
"Who attains nirvāṇa? According to the sūtra, who is it that attains this nirvāṇa?"
The internal [opponent] says:
There is the *sūtra* titled "Attaining Nirvāṇa.
I have previously stated that it is like the extinguishing of a lamp; one cannot say that it goes to the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, or below.
Nirvāṇa is also like this: all speech ceases, and there is nothing that can be discussed or described.
This is non-existence; who could possibly attain it?
Even if there were a nirvāṇa, there would still be no one to attain it.
If the self were to attain nirvana, then because the self is eternal and omnipresent, it should not be able to attain nirvana.
The five aggregates, likewise, cannot attain nirvana. Why is this?
Because the five aggregates are impermanent and because the five aggregates arise and perish,
to whom would such nirvana belong?
If one says that nirvana is attained, this is spoken from within the world of saṃsāra.
Chapter Ten: Refuting Emptiness (Śūnyatā-vibhaṅga-parivarta). The opponent says:
There must be various dharmas because there is a refutation of existence.
If they did not exist, how could there be a sūtra that refutes other dharmas by means of existence?
You have refuted the characteristics of all phenomena; if this refutation itself exists, one should not say that all phenomena are empty, because of the existence of that refutation.
Since that refutation exists, it cannot be called the refutation of all phenomena.
If there were no refutation, all phenomena would exist.
The internal [proponent] says:
Refutation is like that which is to be refuted, as stated in the Sūtra.
Because you are attached to "destruction," you wish to destroy this very destruction by means of existence and non-existence.
Do you not know that because destruction is established, all phenomena are empty and non-existent?
If this refutation exists, it has already fallen within the category of that which is to be refuted and is thus empty and non-existent.
If this refutation does not exist, what is there for you to refute?
It is as when one says there is no second head; it does not come into existence simply because of the act of refuting it.
